title: How to Build an AI Voice Agent: Speech-to-Speech, Tool Calling, and Latency Explained
author: Aishwarya Srinivasan
content_html:
A voice agent sounds simple: the user talks, the AI talks back. Under the hood it is one of the most demanding things you can build, because voice has no loading spinner. People notice a half-second of silence and start talking over it. Getting a voice agent to feel natural is a fight against latency at every stage, plus the harder problem of letting it actually do things through tool calls while still responding in real time. This post is about how voice agents are built, the two architectures you can pick, and the latency budget that makes or breaks the experience.

Think about what makes a phone conversation feel natural versus awkward. It is timing. When you finish a sentence, the other person starts within a fraction of a second. If they pause too long, you assume the line dropped and start repeating yourself. Now imagine the other person is an AI that has to: notice you stopped talking, convert your speech to text, think about a reply, maybe look something up, write the reply, and convert it back to speech, all before that awkward silence kicks in. A voice agent is a relay race against the clock where every runner has to be fast, because the finish line is the roughly one second of silence a human will tolerate before it feels broken. Everything in building voice agents comes back to winning that race.*

Text chat forgives slowness. A chatbot can think for three seconds and nobody minds, because they are watching a spinner and reading at their own pace. Voice forgives nothing. Human conversation runs on turn-taking gaps of a couple hundred milliseconds, and once the gap stretches past roughly a second, the whole thing feels stilted, people interrupt, and the illusion of talking to something intelligent collapses. So a voice agent is fundamentally a latency engineering problem wearing an AI costume. This post walks the full pipeline, the two ways to architect it, how tool calling fits without wrecking the timing, and how to budget the milliseconds.

For a visual deep-dive check out my YouTube video as well:

1. The Pipeline: What Happens Between “You Talk” and “It Talks”

Start with the full journey of a single spoken exchange, because every design choice is about compressing this sequence.

Six stages. First, voice activity detection (VAD) decides when the user has actually finished speaking, not just paused mid-thought. Then speech-to-text (STT, also called ASR) turns the audio into words. Then the LLM reads those words and produces a reply, possibly calling a tool along the way. Then text-to-speech (TTS) turns the reply back into audio. Then the agent speaks, and the loop repeats. Every one of these stages costs time, and they traditionally run in sequence, so the total latency is the sum. The entire craft of voice agents is making this sum small enough to stay under the human silence threshold, and the first big fork in the road is whether you keep these as separate stages at all.

2. The Hard Problem Is Turn-Taking

Before architecture, understand the subtlest stage, because it is the one that quietly ruins otherwise good voice agents: knowing when the user is done talking.

Humans pause mid-sentence constantly: to think, to breathe, to say “um.” An agent that treats every pause as “your turn is over” will interrupt people constantly. An agent that waits to be sure will feel sluggish. This is the endpointing problem, deciding the exact moment a turn ends, and it is a real engineering challenge, not a solved checkbox. Naive systems use a fixed silence timer (say, wait 700ms of quiet), which is a blunt instrument: too short and it interrupts, too long and it lags. Better systems use smarter signals, including the semantic content (does the sentence sound grammatically complete?) to decide faster. The reason this matters so much is that endpointing latency is pure overhead added before the agent even starts thinking, and it is the stage people most often forget to budget for. Get endpointing wrong and no amount of fast STT or TTS will save the feel of the conversation.

3. Architecture One: The Cascaded Pipeline (STT to LLM to TTS)

The classic way to build a voice agent chains three specialized models together: speech-to-text, then a language model, then text-to-speech. This is the cascaded (or pipeline) architecture.

The appeal here is control and flexibility. Each stage is a swappable component: you pick the best STT, the best LLM for your logic, the best-sounding TTS voice, and you can mix vendors. You get a clean text transcript for free (useful for logging, analytics, and tool calling), and you can apply all your existing text-based LLM tooling, prompts, and guardrails directly. The cost is latency and lost information. Latency, because you are paying for three sequential model calls plus the handoffs between them. Lost information, because when speech becomes text, you throw away how it was said, the tone, the emotion, the hesitation, so the LLM only sees flat words and the TTS has to guess at delivery. For most production voice agents today, cascaded is still the workhorse, because the control and the clean transcript are worth a lot, and streaming (section 8) hides much of the latency. But it has a ceiling, and that ceiling is what the second architecture breaks through.

4. Architecture Two: Speech-to-Speech Models

The newer approach collapses the pipeline into a single model that takes audio in and produces audio out directly, with no text stage in the middle. This is the speech-to-speech (or “realtime,” or native audio) architecture.

Because there is no conversion to text and back, two things improve. Latency drops, since you are running one model instead of three sequential ones with handoffs. And the model can perceive and produce the full richness of speech, tone, emotion, pace, laughter, interruptions, because that information is never flattened into text. A speech-to-speech model can hear that you sound frustrated and respond gently, which a cascaded pipeline literally cannot, because by the time its LLM sees your words, the frustration has been deleted. The tradeoffs are the mirror image of cascaded’s strengths: you give up fine-grained control over each stage, you may not get a clean text transcript as easily (so logging, moderation, and tool integration can be trickier), and you are tied to whatever model provides the capability. Speech-to-speech is where the field is heading for naturalness, but it is less mature and less controllable than the cascaded approach, which is exactly the choice you have to make.

5. Choosing Between Them

The decision is not about which is “better” in the abstract; it is about what your application needs most. Here is the honest tradeoff.

  • Choose cascaded when control matters most: complex business logic, strict guardrails and moderation, detailed logging and analytics, the need to swap components or vendors, or heavy tool use that benefits from a clean transcript.

  • Choose speech-to-speech when the experience is the product: a companion, a natural conversational assistant, anything where emotional nuance and sub-second responsiveness beat fine control.

Many teams start cascaded because it is easier to reason about and debug, then move toward speech-to-speech as those models mature and as naturalness becomes the differentiator. A pragmatic middle path exists too: use speech-to-speech for the conversational feel but still capture a transcript alongside it for logging and tool calling. The key is to make this choice deliberately against your actual requirements, because it shapes everything downstream, including how you handle the next hard problem: tools.

6. Tool Calling Without Killing the Conversation

A voice agent that can only chat is a toy. A useful one books the appointment, checks the order, looks up the account, which means calling tools. The problem: a tool call takes time, and in voice, time is silence, and silence feels broken.

The mechanics of tool calling are the same as in text agents: the model emits a structured request to call a named function with arguments, your code runs it, and the result goes back into the model’s context so it can respond. What changes in voice is that you cannot leave the user in silence while the tool runs. The standard trick is filler speech: the moment the agent decides to call a slow tool, it says something natural like “let me pull that up” and starts speaking while the tool runs in the background, so the user hears life instead of a dead line. You also design tools to be fast and, where possible, to stream partial results. And you think hard about when to call a tool versus answer directly, because every tool call adds a round trip to your latency budget. Tool calling is where voice agents earn their keep, but it is also where the latency budget gets blown, so it has to be designed around the silence problem from the start, not bolted on after.

7. The Latency Budget

Pull it together into the number that governs everything: total round-trip latency, from the user finishing their sentence to the agent’s voice starting. The target is to stay under roughly a second, and ideally near half that for a snappy feel.

Think of it as a budget you spend across stages. Endpointing eats a few hundred milliseconds before anything starts. STT can largely be hidden by transcribing while the user is still talking, so it costs little at the end. The LLM’s time to first token (TTFT, the same prefill latency from the inference discussion) is usually the biggest and most variable chunk, which is why voice agents favor fast models and short prompts. TTS can start speaking the first words before the whole reply is generated, so its first-audio latency is what matters, not the full synthesis time. The discipline is that these add up, and your job is to shave each one: stream everything possible, pick low-latency models, keep prompts tight, and overlap stages instead of running them strictly in sequence. Speech-to-speech wins here by collapsing several of these stages into one. The single most useful habit is to measure the real end-to-end number on real calls, because it is the only metric the user actually feels, and it is usually worse than the sum of the parts you measured in isolation.

title: The AI Engineering Goldmine for 2027
author: Aishwarya Srinivasan
content_html:
The AI Engineering Goldmine: 20 Resources Worth Saving

There’s so much AI content out there that you can spend an entire weekend figuring out what to learn and still never open your code editor.

So I wanted to put a useful starting point in one place.

This collection brings together my videos, hands-on sessions from Gen Academy, and resources from across the industry. I’ve organized it around five things: understanding the roles, building a portfolio, preparing for interviews, learning agentic AI, and going deeper with industry experts.

You don’t need to finish everything here. Start with the section that helps you take your next step.

1. Figure out which AI engineering role interests you

Before you make a learning plan, get a clearer picture of the work you actually want to do. Building AI products, working on ML systems, and helping customers deploy AI can involve quite different day-to-day responsibilities.

These resources will help you explore those directions:

  • 6 AI Engineering Roles in 2026⁠ · My breakdown of the roles.

  • Forward Deployed Engineer: The Hottest AI Job of 2026⁠ · A closer look at forward-deployed engineering.

  • How to Become an AI Engineer⁠ · Udacity’s guide to skills, career paths, and how the role differs from ML engineering.

  • AI Engineering Job Titles Explained⁠ · Agentic Careers.

2. Build something you can talk about in detail

My advice: pick one project and take it far enough that you have something interesting to say about it. Why did you choose that approach? Where did it fail? How did you decide whether it was working?

Those questions make a much better project story than a list of frameworks you used.

  • 5 AI Engineer Projects to Build in 2026⁠ · My video.

  • 5 AI Portfolio Projects for Forward-Deployed Engineers⁠ · My video.

  • Build with Keenable Agent: Web Research in Action⁠ · Gen Academy.

  • Beyond Simple Agents: Building with LangChain Deep Agents⁠ · Gen Academy.

3. Practice explaining your engineering decisions

Use interview questions to find gaps in your understanding. Try answering out loud before reading the solution, and actually write the code when there’s an exercise.

For system design, practice explaining why you would choose one approach and what you would give up by choosing it.

  • Agentic AI System Design Explained in 27 Minutes⁠ · My walkthrough.

  • 114 AI Agent Engineer Interview Questions, Coding Exercises and System Designs⁠ · GitHub.

  • 210 AI Engineering Interview Questions Across 7 Roles⁠ · GitHub.

  • Agentic AI Coding Interview Preparation⁠ · GitHub.

4. Get comfortable with agentic AI

If agents still feel confusing, start with the overview. Then work through retrieval and more advanced agent behavior.

I’ve also included OpenAI’s written guide, which covers when to build an agent, how to structure it, and where guardrails fit.

  • Agentic AI Explained: The Complete 2026 Guide⁠ · My video.

  • Agentic RAG Masterclass⁠ · My video.

  • How to Build Self-Improving AI Agents⁠ · My video.

  • A Practical Guide to Building AI Agents⁠ · OpenAI.

5. Go deeper with Gen Academy Live Labs

Once you’ve built something, you start having more specific questions. How can I improve retrieval? How do I check an agent’s work? Why is this getting so expensive?

That’s where I’d bring in these sessions with industry experts:

  • The RAG Playbook: Retrieval Techniques for Production AI⁠ · Pinecone.

  • Agentic Coding at Scale: Verification Loops That Hold⁠ · Anthropic.

  • Optimize Agent Costs Without Compromising Quality⁠ · Langfuse.

  • AI Tokenomics Explained⁠ · NVIDIA.

Save this for when you need it. But for today, choose one resource, open it, and put something you learn into practice. Even a small, unfinished project gives you questions that another weekend of bookmarking won’t.

title: Recursive Self-Improvement in AI: How Agents Improve Their Own Code and What Limits Them
author: Aishwarya Srinivasan
content_html:
Recursive self-improvement is the idea that an AI could get better at making itself better, each improved version more capable of improving the next, spiraling upward. It is one of the most consequential ideas in AI and also one of the most misunderstood, because it spans two very different things: a concrete engineering loop that agents genuinely run today to improve their own code, and a speculative runaway scenario that may or may not be physically possible. This post separates the two, shows the real mechanism that exists right now, and walks carefully through what actually limits it.

If this interests you then you should check out my YouTube video on building self improving agents from scratch:

Imagine a carpenter who can build tools. With better tools, they build furniture faster. But here is the twist: with better tools, they can also build even better tools, which let them build still better tools, and so on. If each round of better tools makes the next round of tool-building easier, you could imagine the carpenter’s capability snowballing. Recursive self-improvement is that idea applied to intelligence itself: an AI that is good at building AI could build a better AI, which is even better at building AI, and so on, each step compounding. The crucial question, and the whole debate, is whether that snowball actually keeps rolling faster, or whether it hits a hill it cannot climb. This post is about both the snowball and the hill.*

The phrase gets used in two completely different registers and conflating them causes endless confusion. In the near-term, practical register, recursive self-improvement means an AI agent editing its own code, tools, and prompts to get measurably better at its tasks, a real loop that exists and runs today, bounded and modest. In the long-term, speculative register, it means the hypothesized “intelligence explosion,” a chain reaction where a sufficiently capable AI redesigns itself so rapidly that it blows past human intelligence in a short window, a scenario that is genuinely debated and far from established. Both are worth understanding, and keeping them distinct is the first step to thinking clearly about either. This post covers the real mechanism first, then the theoretical dream, then, at length, the walls, because the limits are where the actual intellectual content lives.

  5. Limit One: Validation Is the Bottleneck

1. Two Very Different Meanings

Before anything else, split the term in two, because almost every confused argument about recursive self-improvement is really two people using the same words for different things.

The practical meaning is an agent that measurably improves its own artifacts: it writes a better version of its code, designs a new tool for itself, refines its own prompts or workflows, and verifies that the new version does better on a benchmark. This happens now, in research and increasingly in production, and it is bounded, incremental, and heavily dependent on human-built infrastructure around it. The speculative meaning is the intelligence explosion: a self-reinforcing loop where each smarter version produces an even smarter version faster than the last, rapidly exceeding human capability. That is a hypothesis about the future, actively debated, and not something anyone has demonstrated. When someone says “recursive self-improvement,” your first move should be to ask which one they mean, because the evidence, the stakes, and the right level of skepticism are completely different. The rest of this post treats them in turn and spends most of its time on the limits that apply to both.

2. The Real Loop That Exists Today

Start with what is real, because it grounds the speculation. An AI agent can improve itself today through a concrete, verifiable loop, and it is just the verification loop you already know, pointed back at the agent itself.

If the candidate scores better, it is kept as the new baseline; if not, it is discarded. Then the loop repeats from the improved baseline. This is genuinely recursive in the sense that each accepted improvement becomes the starting point for proposing the next. It is also completely dependent on one thing: a reliable way to measure “better.” That measurement, the evaluation, is both what makes the loop work and, as we will see, the single biggest thing that limits it. Notice what is doing the real work here: not magic, but the same disciplined verification that makes any agent reliable, now applied to the agent’s own definition.

“An agent improves its own code” sounds dramatic, so pin down what it actually refers to, because the reality is more specific and more mundane than the phrase suggests.

It can rewrite its own prompts to get better results, write new tools and functions to extend its reach, restructure its own planning and orchestration logic (the scaffolding or harness), and edit its own source code and strategies. What it generally does not do is reach into the underlying neural network and retrain its own weights from the inside; that remains a separate, resource-intensive process controlled by humans and their training infrastructure. Now the speculative version, stated fairly, because it is a serious idea with serious people on both sides, not a straw man. The intelligence explosion hypothesis says the loop above, if it ever applied to the core capability itself, could run away.

The logic is seductive and simple. Suppose an AI becomes as good as the best humans at the specific task of improving AI. It then designs a better AI. That better AI is, by assumption, even better at the task of improving AI, so it designs a still better one, and faster, because it is more capable. If each generation is produced more quickly and is more capable than the last, capability compounds and could, in principle, shoot past human intelligence in a short span, the “explosion,” sometimes tied to the idea of a technological singularity. This is the scenario that drives a lot of AI-safety concern, and taken on its own terms the internal logic is coherent. The entire question, the hinge on which the whole thing turns, is the assumption buried in the middle: does each step actually get easier, so the loop accelerates, or does each step get harder, so the loop fizzles? That is not a philosophical question; it is an empirical one about where the bottlenecks are, and the next four sections are the reasons many researchers think the loop is far more constrained than the clean diagram suggests.

5. Limit One: Validation Is the Bottleneck

The first and most fundamental limit is the one hiding in plain sight in the real loop: you can only keep an improvement if you can reliably tell it is an improvement, and verifying is often harder than generating.

Self-improvement is only as good as your ability to measure improvement, and measurement is frequently the hard part. When “better” is cheap and reliable to check, the agent passes more unit tests, solves more benchmark problems, runs faster, the loop works beautifully, because you can generate many candidates and let the evaluator sort them. But for most things that matter, “better” is subjective, slow to reveal itself, or expensive to measure, and then the evaluator, not the generator, becomes the binding constraint. An agent can propose a thousand improvements per hour, but if validating each one requires expensive real-world testing or human judgment, your throughput collapses to the speed of validation. Worse, if your evaluator is flawed or gameable, the agent will happily “improve” by exploiting the metric rather than getting genuinely better, optimizing the measure instead of the thing the measure was supposed to track. This is why validation, not idea generation, is widely seen as the real bottleneck on self-improvement, and it is a bottleneck that does not obviously shrink as the agent gets smarter, because judging quality can be fundamentally harder than producing candidates.

6. Limit Two: Diminishing Returns and Compute

The intelligence-explosion diagram assumes each step gets easier. The second limit is the strong possibility that each step actually gets harder, and that the whole thing is gated by physical resources that do not spiral.

Progress in most hard domains shows diminishing returns: the easy improvements come first and cheaply, and each further gain costs disproportionately more effort than the last. If self-improvement works that way, and there is good reason to think intelligence is a hard domain, then the loop decelerates rather than accelerates, because each smarter version faces a harder remaining problem that exactly offsets, or more than offsets, its greater capability. On top of that sits the brute physical fact of compute. Meaningfully more capable AI has, so far, required vastly more computation to train and run, and compute is physical: it needs chips, power, cooling, data centers, and money, none of which an agent can conjure by thinking harder. An AI cannot simply reason its way into more GPUs; acquiring them is a slow, expensive, real-world process bounded by supply chains and physics. So even an agent that is brilliant at designing improvements may be throttled by its inability to get the compute to train or run them. The clean explosion diagram quietly assumes resources are free and returns are constant or increasing; both assumptions are, at minimum, highly questionable, and if either fails the snowball stops rolling.

7. Limit Three: The Ceiling of Self-Generated Data

The third limit concerns what the AI learns from. A system improving itself tends to be learning from its own outputs, and there are real questions about how far that can go before it runs out of genuinely new signal.

Learning requires new information, and an AI improving itself largely from its own generated data faces a ceiling: you cannot bootstrap genuinely new knowledge about the world purely from what you already contain. There is a documented failure mode, sometimes called model collapse, where systems trained predominantly on their own outputs degrade over successive generations, losing fidelity rather than gaining it, because each round amplifies the model’s existing blind spots instead of correcting them. Real, grounded improvement in most domains requires contact with reality: fresh data, actual experiments whose outcomes the AI did not already know, and feedback from the external world, including humans. That contact is inherently slow and external; you cannot speed up the physical experiment, the real market, or the human response by being smarter. So the kinds of self-improvement that stay purely internal (refining reasoning, optimizing known objectives) can run fast, but the kinds that require learning something genuinely new about the world are rate-limited by reality itself, which does not accelerate just because the AI does. This caps how far a closed self-improvement loop can go without opening a window onto the slow, external world.

content_html:
If you want to learn AI engineering in 2027, here’s where I’d suggest starting: understand how an agent works, learn how to design the application around it, and get comfortable evaluating what you’ve built.

Then bring those skills together in a project you can explain.

I’ve put together four videos from my YouTube channel that I recommend watching in this order. Each addresses a different part of building AI systems, and I’ll walk you through what to focus on as you watch.

My suggestion is to keep one project in mind throughout. It could be a support assistant that answers questions from product documentation, for example. As you move through the resources, you’ll have a concrete place to apply what you’re learning.

You don’t have to finish the entire watchlist before you start building. In fact, I’d encourage you to pause between videos and try things out. The questions that come up while you build will make the next resource much more useful.

A quick note on where to begin

This watchlist assumes some familiarity with Python, APIs, SQL, Git, testing, and debugging. If those are still new to you, spend time on them alongside these resources.

You should be able to make an API request, inspect the response, and work out why something failed. Those skills carry directly into AI engineering. When your assistant returns a poor answer, you’ll need to investigate the application, the retrieved information, and the model’s response.

With that foundation, here’s the learning path I’d recommend.

1. Start by understanding AI agents

Watch: AI Agents Explained in 14 Minutes (The Complete Guide)

I’d start here if you’ve heard terms like agents, workflows, tools, and orchestration, but aren’t quite sure how they fit together.

This video introduces the components of an agent, different execution patterns, and common frameworks. As you watch, pay particular attention to how the system decides what to do next. That’s the part I want you to be able to explain before you choose a framework.

Take our support assistant. You could define a fixed sequence: receive a question, search the documentation, and generate an answer from the relevant passages. The application controls those steps.

You could also give the model some choice over what happens next. Perhaps it asks a clarifying question, searches another source, or decides that it needs help from a person.

That choice should come from the task you’re trying to solve. What does the extra flexibility allow the application to do? And what additional behavior will you need to test?

Here’s what I’d like you to try after watching: write down your project’s goal, the information it can access, the tools it can use, and when it should stop. Then explain whether you need a fixed workflow or an agent.

If you can make that decision and explain your reasoning, you’ve taken something useful from the video.

2. Learn how to design the complete system

Watch: Agentic AI System Design Explained in 27 Minutes

Once the agent concepts make sense, I’d move to system design. This is especially useful if you’ve built a small AI demo and are wondering how to turn it into an application someone else can use.

The question to keep in mind is: what needs to happen around the model call?

For the support assistant, your application needs to receive the user’s question, find relevant documentation, provide that context to the model, and display the answer. You also need to think about authentication, logging, and deployment.

I recommend watching this with a blank page open. Draw the path of one request through your application. Mark where information comes from and where something could go wrong.

For example, retrieving no useful documentation is different from the documentation service being unavailable. In the first case, the answer may not exist in your source material. In the second, the application couldn’t access it. You’ll want enough information in your logs to tell the difference.

And think about the person using the product. What do they see when the system can’t answer? Can they retry? Is there a clear route to support?

After this video, aim to have an architecture diagram you can walk someone through. Pick a few decisions and write down why you made them. A narrow first version is completely reasonable, as long as you understand its limits.

3. Spend time learning AI evaluations

Watch: AI Evals Explained | How to evaluate AI Agents?

This is the resource I’d encourage you to return to while you’re building.

It’s easy to try a few questions, like the answers, and feel that your application is working. But when you change the prompt or the retrieval setup, how will you know whether it actually improved?

That’s why I want you to learn evaluations early. You need examples you can test repeatedly, with a clear definition of the behavior you expect.

The video covers evaluation metrics, golden datasets, grading methods, and continuous evaluation. A golden dataset is a curated reference set of examples with expected answers or behavior that you can use to assess your system.

Start small. For our support assistant, I’d include a question the documentation answers clearly, a question it doesn’t cover, and a request that needs clarification.

For “How do I reset my password?”, the expected behavior depends on the evidence available. If the documentation includes the instructions, the assistant should explain them accurately. If it doesn’t, the assistant should acknowledge the gap or escalate.

That distinction matters. A fluent answer can still be unsupported.

As you work through the video, think about which checks you can automate and which need human judgment. Record the actual answer, whether it was supported, whether the task succeeded, response time, and model cost.

My recommendation: create your first test set before you feel the project is finished. Rerun it when you make changes, and add cases whenever you discover a new failure. You’ll have a much clearer basis for deciding what to improve next.

4. Choose a project that brings these skills together

Watch: 5 AI Engineer Projects to Build in 2026 | Ex-Google, Microsoft

Yes, the title says 2026. I’m recommending it for your 2027 learning plan because the exercise still applies: choose a problem, build a usable solution, and show the engineering behind it.

Use this video to explore project directions. You don’t need to build all five. I’d rather you choose one that interests you enough to keep working on it when the first version doesn’t behave as expected.

Define who it’s for and what a useful first version would do. Then build, evaluate, and document that version before expanding the scope.

When you present the project, help someone understand your decisions. Include setup instructions, an architecture diagram, and evaluation results. Explain what your application handles well and where it still needs help.

I’d also include a failure example in your walkthrough. Show what went wrong, how you investigated it, and what happened after you made a change. That gives someone a much better view of how you think as an engineer.

For the support assistant, you should be able to explain where its answers come from, how you test them, and when it hands the task back to a person.

How I’d use this watchlist

Watch the first video, then write down your workflow or agent decision. Use the system design video to sketch the application around it. As soon as you have something running, start applying the evaluation concepts. Use the project resource to help you shape and present the work.

You can revisit these in whatever order your project needs. If your tests expose a retrieval problem, go back to the architecture. If the agent keeps taking unnecessary steps, revisit whether it needs that much autonomy.

These four resources give you a focused starting point. The deeper learning comes from making a decision, testing it, and understanding why it worked or failed.

My suggestion for this week: choose one project, watch the first resource, and write a short explanation of what you’re going to build. Keep it specific enough that you can start.

Which part are you working on right now: understanding agents, designing systems, evaluating them, or building your portfolio? Let me know in the comments.

title: How to be human in the Age of AI? ft. Reid Hoffman (co-founder- LinkedIn, Manas AI)
author: Aishwarya Srinivasan
content_html:
An AI agent writes the code. A senior engineer spends the afternoon reviewing it. The next morning, there is more code waiting.

During my conversation with Reid Hoffman at the Masters of Scale Summit, I brought up a concern I hear from engineering managers: generating software has become easier, but the review queue keeps growing. If every new agent creates more work for a person to approve, where is the productivity gain?

AI with Aish is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Reid’s answer opens up a bigger question about working with AI. As execution becomes easier, we have to get much more deliberate about where human attention goes.

That applies to a team reviewing code. It also applies to a founder evaluating an investment, a hiring manager reading applications, or a writer deciding which idea deserves an essay. Producing something plausible is one capability. Recognizing what matters in a particular situation is another.

My takeaway from our conversation: the useful unit of AI productivity is a completed outcome you can stand behind. The workflow has to include the decisions, checks, and corrections that get you there.

Watch our full conversation here.

More output can move the bottleneck

When I asked Reid about the burden of human review, he resisted the idea that there is a permanent balance between autonomy and oversight. Capabilities change. People learn how to use them. Organizations have different responsibilities and tolerances for mistakes. The working arrangement has to keep changing too. Watch this exchange, starting at 5:12.

He drew a useful distinction between a human participating inside the work and a human overseeing work as it proceeds. An agent might continue with routine steps, then pause when it needs a decision or flag a question while completing other tasks.

That sounds straightforward until you try to design it. Which decisions can proceed? Which require approval? What information does the reviewer need? And can the system recognize the situations where it should ask for help?

Here is how I would translate that into a software workflow. An agent could prepare a small change, run tests, and assemble the evidence a reviewer needs. A person would still decide whether a change to permissions or customer data should go ahead. The review would focus on the consequential decision, with supporting evidence already organized.

The distinction matters because an approval button alone does very little. A person facing an enormous queue can become a rubber stamp. Useful oversight requires manageable work, clear escalation rules, and enough context to challenge the result.

A good list is different from a good decision

Later, Reid described using AI for investment research. It can help produce a due-diligence checklist and examine competitors, particularly when the relevant information is public. His concern is what happens when you ask it to identify the few issues that actually determine the decision. Watch at 17:03.

The important issue may appear somewhere in the answer. That does not mean the model has understood its importance.

Reid put the question plainly:

“What’s the one thing here that most matters?”

Imagine evaluating a new business. A model might give you a polished analysis of market size, competitors, pricing, distribution, and technical differentiation. All reasonable topics. But perhaps the business depends on access to data it has no right to use. Or customers like the product, but no one owns the budget to buy it.

Those are illustrative examples, not investments Reid discussed. They show the distinction he was making: an exhaustive answer can still leave the decisive question unresolved.

For anyone building with AI, this suggests a better review habit. Before asking for more analysis, write down the decision you need to make and the evidence that would change it. Then assess the output against that question. Length and confidence are poor substitutes for relevance.

Reid applies a similar test to his AI counterpart, Reid AI. He periodically checks whether it can offer the entrepreneurship advice he would want to give. In his assessment, it can help in some situations, but identifying the most useful intervention for a particular person remains inconsistent. Watch at 20:41.

This is his account of the systems he has tried, not a universal benchmark. It is also a useful reminder to evaluate AI on the decisions your work actually requires.

title: How Memory in AI Agents Work?
author: Aishwarya Srinivasan
content_html:
A language model does not remember your last message, let alone last week. Its weights are frozen and it is stateless between calls. So every agent that seems to “know you,” recall past work, or get better at your codebase over time is running a memory system bolted on the outside: something that decides what to write down, where to store it, how to pull the right piece back, and when to forget. This post is about that system, which is quietly one of the hardest and most important parts of building agents that are actually useful past a single conversation.

Here is the fact that makes memory necessary, and it follows directly from how inference works: a trained model’s weights are frozen, so nothing you say to it is retained in the model. Each call is independent. The only reason a chatbot appears to follow a conversation at all is that the entire history is re-sent in the prompt every single turn. That trick works for one conversation. It falls apart the moment you want an agent to remember across sessions, or to accumulate knowledge over weeks, or to simply handle more context than fits in a single prompt. At that point you need real memory, and real memory is an engineering system, not a model feature.

This post builds that system up from first principles. Why statelessness forces the problem, the difference between the context window (working memory) and persistent memory, the four kinds of memory worth distinguishing, the read-write-forget machinery underneath, how memory differs from RAG even though they share plumbing, and the architectures people actually use. By the end, “give the agent memory” should decompose into concrete decisions rather than being a single magic checkbox.

1. The Root Cause: Models Are Stateless

Start with why memory is even a problem, because it is not obvious. The model is stateless: its weights do not change when you talk to it, and it keeps nothing between calls. A conversation feels continuous only because the whole transcript is fed back in on every turn.

This re-send trick has a hard ceiling: the context window. Everything the model can “see” on a given call, the system prompt, the history, the retrieved documents, your new message, has to fit in that finite window, and every token in it costs money and time to process. So you cannot just keep stuffing more history in forever. The transcript grows, the window fills, and you are forced to choose what to keep and what to drop. The moment you are choosing what to carry forward and what to let go, you are building a memory system, whether you call it that or not. Statelessness is the disease; memory is the treatment.

2. Working Memory vs Persistent Memory

The first useful split is between two layers, and they map cleanly onto a distinction you already know from computers: fast-but-small versus slow-but-large.

Working memory is the context window itself: what the model can directly act on this call. It is fast because the model sees it immediately, but it is small, expensive (every token costs), and volatile (it vanishes when the call ends). Persistent memory is an external store, a database, files, a vector index, that is effectively unbounded and durable but slow, in the sense that nothing in it affects the model until it is retrieved and placed into the context window. The whole game of agent memory is managing the flow between these two: pulling the right things up from persistent store into working memory when needed, and writing the things worth keeping back down before they are lost. If that sounds like a computer’s RAM-and-disk hierarchy, that is exactly the analogy the best-known memory systems are built on, and we will come back to it.

3. The Four Kinds of Memory

“Memory” is one word covering several different things an agent needs to remember, and they want different treatment. Borrowing loosely from how people talk about human memory gives a taxonomy that is genuinely useful for design.

  1. Working (short-term) memory is the current task and recent turns, living in the context window.

  2. Episodic memory is specific past events: what happened, when, and what was decided, the raw material of “remember when we tried X and it broke.”

  3. Semantic memory is distilled facts and knowledge about the user and the world: preferences, names, settled constraints, the kind of thing that belongs in a stable profile rather than a dated log.

  4. Procedural memory is learned how-to: workflows, tool-use recipes, and reusable skills the agent has figured out and should not have to rediscover.


    The reason the split matters is that each kind is written, stored, and retrieved differently. Episodic memory wants timestamps and summaries of events; semantic memory wants deduplicated, updatable facts; procedural memory wants reusable instructions you load when a matching task appears. Lumping them into one undifferentiated “memory” blob is the most common way memory systems get vague and unreliable. A good system usually keeps them in separate stores with separate rules.

4. The Machinery: Write, Store, Retrieve, Inject

Underneath any memory system, regardless of taxonomy, is the same four-step loop. Getting a clear picture of these four stages is most of understanding the whole field, because every framework is just a particular set of choices for each stage.

  • Write is deciding what, out of everything that just happened, is worth saving (and the honest answer is usually “not the raw transcript”).

  • Store is putting it somewhere durable in a form you can search later, a vector index for fuzzy semantic lookup, a key-value store or structured database for exact facts, plain files, or a graph for relationships.

  • Retrieve is finding the right pieces when a new task arrives, which is a search problem.

  • Inject is placing the retrieved pieces into the context window so the model can actually use them, because remember, nothing in persistent store does anything until it is in the prompt.

The loop closes when the new interaction, informed by memory, itself produces things worth writing back. Every “agent with memory” is some concrete implementation of these four arrows.

5. The Hard Part Is Writing, Not Storing

Here is the counterintuitive bit that separates toy memory from working memory. Storage is easy; databases are a solved problem. The hard, unsolved, judgment-heavy part is the write step: deciding what is worth remembering at all, and in what form.

If you write everything verbatim, the store bloats, retrieval gets noisy, and you pay to haul irrelevant junk into the context window. If you write nothing, you have no memory. The art is in the middle: extract the durable facts rather than the chatter (”the user prefers metric units” is worth keeping; “thanks, that’s helpful” is not), summarize events instead of storing raw transcripts, and crucially, update existing memory rather than blindly appending. If the agent already knows you live in Berlin and you mention you moved to Munich, the right move is to revise the fact, not to store two contradictory ones and leave retrieval to flip a coin. This write step is often itself done by a model: a separate pass reads the interaction and decides what to extract, summarize, update, or discard. It is also where things most often go wrong, because deciding what matters is genuinely hard, and an over-eager writer that saves too much poisons retrieval just as surely as one that saves too little.

6. Retrieval: Getting the Right Page Back

Once memory is stored, you have to find the relevant pieces when they matter, and only those pieces, because the context window is finite and expensive. This is a search problem, and it is close kin to retrieval in RAG.

The dominant technique is semantic search: memories are stored as embeddings (vectors capturing meaning), the incoming query is embedded too, and you pull the memories whose vectors are closest in meaning, not just those sharing keywords. Good systems blend that with recency (a memory from an hour ago often beats one from a year ago) and importance (a core fact like a critical preference should surface even when not obviously similar to the current query). Then you take the top handful and inject only those. The discipline here is the same as in tokenomics: context is a scarce, paid resource, so retrieving the right three memories beats retrieving fifty, both for cost and for quality, since a model drowning in marginally-relevant memories reasons worse, not better. Retrieval quality, not storage size, is what makes a memory system feel sharp or sloppy.

7. Memory vs RAG: Same Plumbing, Different Job

Because both lean on vector search and both inject retrieved text into the context, memory and RAG get conflated constantly. They share plumbing but do different jobs, and keeping them distinct clarifies a lot.

RAG retrieves from an external body of knowledge, documentation, a wiki, a product catalog, so the agent can ground its answers in facts it was not trained on. The corpus is authored, shared across users, and mostly read-only. Memoryretrieves the agent’s own accumulated experience and state: what this user said, what this agent did and decided, how a past task went. It is personal, it grows from use, and it is read and written. A clean way to hold it: RAG is the agent looking things up in a shared library; memory is the agent consulting its own private diary. They often coexist in the same agent and even share a vector database, but conflating them leads to muddled design, like storing another user’s shared documents in the same place as this user’s private preferences and losing track of which is which.

8. Forgetting, Updating, and Consolidation

A memory system that only ever grows eventually collapses under its own weight: retrieval slows, noise rises, and stale or contradictory facts pile up. So forgetting is not a bug to be minimized, it is a feature to be designed, exactly as it is in humans.

Four moves keep a store healthy.

  1. Update: when a fact changes, revise it rather than storing a duplicate.

  2. Expire: let time-bound facts (a branch name, a temporary status) fall away instead of lingering as traps.

  3. Consolidate: periodically compress a pile of episodic events into a compact semantic summary, the same way sleep is thought to turn a day’s experiences into durable knowledge, so you keep the lesson without the raw log.

  4. Resolve conflicts: when two memories disagree, have a rule, usually prefer the newer or higher-confidence one, rather than surfacing both and letting the model guess.

These are the operations that separate a memory system you can trust after six months from one that quietly rots. And they are hard precisely because they require judgment about what is still true, which is why consolidation and conflict resolution are often themselves model-driven passes rather than simple database rules.

title: Vector Database Indexing Explained: HNSW vs IVF, Recall, and Search Latency
author: Aishwarya Srinivasan
content_html:
Every RAG system, every semantic search box, every “find me similar” feature rests on one operation: given a query vector, find the closest vectors out of millions. Done naively, that means comparing the query against every single vector, which is far too slow at scale. Vector database indexing is the set of clever tricks that make this fast by agreeing to be approximately right instead of exactly right. This post explains how the two dominant index families (HNSW and IVF) actually work, what “recall” means and why you are always trading it against speed and memory, and how to reason about the knobs.

Here is the problem stated plainly. A vector is a list of numbers that captures the meaning of something (a sentence, an image, a user) so that similar things have nearby vectors. Search means: given a query vector, find its nearest neighbors among your stored vectors. The exact method, compare the query to all N vectors and sort, is called brute-force or flat search, and it is perfectly accurate but scales linearly: ten times the data, ten times the time. At a few thousand vectors that is fine. At ten million it is hopeless for anything real-time. title: Agentic RAG, Explained and Built
author: Aishwarya Srinivasan
content_html:
Traditional RAG retrieves once and answers. Agentic RAG decides what to retrieve, checks whether it is enough, retrieves again, and stops when it actually has the answer. That difference is the whole leap from a search box to a researcher. Here is how both work, when each is right, and how to build the agentic version without it running forever.

Old-style RAG is like handing someone a single stack of photocopies and asking them to answer from exactly that stack, no more, no less. Agentic RAG is like giving a smart research assistant a library card: they read the question, decide what to look up, go find it, notice “this does not fully answer it,” look up the missing piece, and only then write the answer. The assistant is more capable, but it can also wander the stacks forever or pull the same book twice, so the real engineering is giving it a clear goal, a way to check its own work, and a rule for when to stop.

https://maven.com/aishwarya-srinivasan/mastering-ai-agents

Retrieval-augmented generation was the fix for a real problem: language models do not know your private documents and confidently make things up about things they half-remember. Classic RAG solved that by fetching relevant chunks of your data and handing them to the model as context. It works, and for a huge number of use cases it is still the right, cheap answer.

But classic RAG has a ceiling, and you hit it the moment a question needs more than one lookup, or a decision about where to look, or a check on whether the retrieved material is actually sufficient. Agentic RAG raises that ceiling by wrapping retrieval in an agent: a loop that reasons about the question, chooses retrieval actions, observes what came back, and decides whether to retrieve again or answer.

This post covers both ends of that spectrum, the ReAct loop and reflection, the harness that holds it together, chunking and vector search, query decomposition and multi-hop retrieval, reranking candidate chunks with a System 1 model like Jev, and the permissions, verification, and stopping conditions that keep an agentic system safe and finite. With code, and a travel-assistant example to make it concrete.

Index

  1. Models, Agents, and Harnesses, Quickly

  2. Traditional RAG: The Foundation You Still Need

  3. Chunking Strategies and Vector Search

  4. The ReAct Pattern and Reflection

  5. Traditional RAG vs Agentic RAG

  6. Query Decomposition, Routing, and Multi-Hop Retrieval

  7. A Travel Assistant, Step by Step, in LlamaIndex

  8. Reranking Candidate Chunks With Jev

  9. Permissions, Verification, Duplicate Prevention, and Stopping Conditions

  10. When to Use a Simple Pipeline vs an Agent

  11. Linkstash

1. Models, Agents, and Harnesses, Quickly

Three words get used loosely, so pin them down before anything else, because agentic RAG is built out of all three.

A model is the raw reasoning: you give it text, it gives you text. An agent is a model placed in a loop where it can take actions (call a retriever, call a tool), see the results, and decide what to do next. A harness is everything around that loop that makes it work in production: the tools it is allowed to use, how its context and memory are managed, its permissions, and the rules that make it stop. In agentic RAG, retrieval is one of the tools in the harness, and the agent is the thing deciding when and how to use it. Keep this layering in mind; every later section slots into one of these three.

2. Traditional RAG: The Foundation You Still Need

Do not skip the classic pipeline, because agentic RAG is built on top of it, not instead of it. Traditional RAG is a fixed, linear sequence: embed the query, search a vector store for similar chunks, stuff the top matches into the prompt, and generate an answer.

This is one retrieval, one generation, no decisions. Its strengths are real: it is simple, fast, cheap, predictable, and easy to debug, and for a well-scoped corpus answering direct questions it is often all you need. Its limits are equally real. It always retrieves exactly once, so a question needing two facts from two places is already beyond it. It cannot decide that the retrieved chunks are irrelevant and try again. It cannot choose between data sources. And it has no notion of “that was not enough.” Every limitation agentic RAG removes is a limitation of this fixed shape, so understanding the shape is the foundation.

3. Chunking Strategies and Vector Search

Retrieval quality is set before the agent ever runs, by how you split your documents and how you search them. Get this layer wrong and no amount of agentic cleverness recovers it.

  • Chunking is splitting documents into pieces small enough to retrieve precisely but large enough to carry meaning. The naive approach, fixed-size chunks, is easy and often cuts a sentence or an idea in half. Better approaches split on structure (headings, paragraphs) and meaning, and add a little overlap between chunks so an idea sitting on a boundary is not lost. The right chunk size is a genuine tradeoff: small chunks are precise but fragmentary, large chunks carry context but dilute relevance and cost more tokens.

  • Vector search is how retrieval finds the right chunks. Each chunk is turned into an embedding (a vector that captures its meaning), the query is embedded the same way, and the store returns the chunks whose vectors are nearest. The crucial 2026 refinement, which carries straight into the agentic version, is that pure vector similarity is no longer the best you can do. Hybrid retrieval, combining semantic vector search with keyword search, plus a reranking step over the candidates, beats vector-only on almost every real workload. Hold that reranking thought; Jev enters there in section 8.

4. The ReAct Pattern and Reflection

Here is the engine of agentic behavior, and it is simpler than it sounds. ReAct stands for Reason, Act, Observe, a loop the agent runs until it is done.

Each turn, the agent reasons about what it knows and what it still needs, acts by calling a tool (in RAG, usually a retriever), and observes the result. Then it decides: is this enough to answer, or do I loop again? That loop is the entire difference between a search box and a researcher. The search box runs the pipeline once; the ReAct agent keeps pulling the thread until the question is actually answered.

Reflection is the safety valve on top. When the agent notices it is stuck, repeating itself, or getting irrelevant results, a reflection step asks it to step back and critique its own approach before trying again, rather than grinding the same failing action. Reason-Act-Observe gives the agent forward motion; reflection keeps that motion from becoming an infinite loop of the same mistake. Both are cheap to add and transform reliability.

5. Traditional RAG vs Agentic RAG

Now put the two side by side, because choosing between them is the most consequential decision in the whole design.

Traditional RAG is a straight line: one retrieval, one answer. Agentic RAG is a loop with judgment inside it: the agent decides whether to retrieve, what to retrieve, from which source, and whether what came back is sufficient, looping until it is. The agentic version handles questions that need multiple facts, comparisons across sources, lookups that depend on earlier lookups, and cases where the first retrieval misses. The cost is real and worth stating plainly: agentic RAG is slower, more expensive (every loop is more model calls and more tokens, which compounds exactly as the context tax predicts), and harder to debug. The engineering judgment is knowing which questions actually need the loop, and section 10 is about exactly that.

6. Query Decomposition, Routing, and Multi-Hop Retrieval

Three specific agentic capabilities do most of the heavy lifting, and they are worth naming precisely because they are where agentic RAG earns its cost

  • Query decomposition breaks a complex question into simpler sub-questions the system can answer separately, then combines them. “What is the best time to visit Japan and what should I pack” is really two questions, and splitting them retrieves far better than treating the mix as one search.

  • Routing sends each question to the right source. Weather goes to a weather index, visa rules to the policy documents, hotel availability to a bookings database. A traditional pipeline has one source and no choice; the agent picks the right tool for each part.

  • Multi-hop retrieval chains lookups where each answer feeds the next. “What are the must-see events in the capital of the country hosting the next World Cup” cannot be answered in one search, you first retrieve the host country, then its capital, then events there. Each hop depends on the previous one, which is impossible for single-shot RAG and natural for a ReAct loop. These three are the capabilities that justify going agentic.

7. A Travel Assistant, Step by Step, in LlamaIndex

Make it concrete with a travel assistant, the kind of query that genuinely needs the agentic loop: “I have four days in Japan in April, plan it around the cherry blossoms, I am vegetarian, and keep it under a budget.” That is decomposition, routing, and multi-hop all at once. LlamaIndex Workflows are a clean way to build it, because a workflow is an event-driven graph of typed steps, which matches the Reason-Act-Observe loop directly.

Here is the shape in LlamaIndex Workflows. The types are the diagram: each step consumes one event and emits another, and the loop-back is just a step that can emit either a “need more” event or a “done” event.

from llama_index.core.workflow import (
    Workflow, step, Context, StartEvent, StopEvent, Event
)

class SubQuestions(Event):
    questions: list[str]

class Retrieved(Event):
    chunks: list[dict]      # each: {text, source, score}

class Reflected(Event):
    sufficient: bool
    missing: list[str]

class AgenticRAG(Workflow):
    @step
    async def plan(self, ctx: Context, ev: StartEvent) -> SubQuestions:
        await ctx.store.set("query", ev.query)
        await ctx.store.set("seen_ids", set())          # for duplicate prevention
        subs = await decompose(ev.query)                # LLM: split into parts
        return SubQuestions(questions=subs)

    @step
    async def retrieve(self, ctx: Context, ev: SubQuestions) -> Retrieved:
        seen = await ctx.store.get("seen_ids")
        chunks = []
        for q in ev.questions:
            source = route(q)                           # pick the right index
            hits = hybrid_search(source, q, k=20)       # semantic + keyword
            for h in hits:
                if h["id"] not in seen:                 # skip duplicates
                    seen.add(h["id"])
                    chunks.append(h)
        await ctx.store.set("seen_ids", seen)
        return Retrieved(chunks=chunks)

    @step
    async def reflect(self, ctx: Context, ev: Retrieved) -> Reflected | StopEvent:
        hops = await ctx.store.get("hops", default=0)
        reranked = rerank(ev.chunks)[:8]                # Jev reranking, section 8
        await ctx.store.set("context", reranked)
        judgment = await assess_sufficiency(            # reflection step
            await ctx.store.get("query"), reranked)
        # stopping conditions: answered, or out of hops
        if judgment.sufficient or hops >= 3:
            answer = await synthesize_and_verify(
                await ctx.store.get("query"), reranked)
            return StopEvent(result=answer)
        await ctx.store.set("hops", hops + 1)
        return Reflected(sufficient=False, missing=judgment.missing)

    @step
    async def replan(self, ctx: Context, ev: Reflected) -> SubQuestions:
        return SubQuestions(questions=ev.missing)       # multi-hop: chase the gaps

Read the steps top to bottom and the whole agentic pattern is visible: plan decomposes, retrieve routes and dedupes, reflect reranks and judges sufficiency, and either stops or loops back through replan to chase what is missing.

The hops >= 3check is the stopping condition that keeps it finite; seen_ids is duplicate prevention; and the whole thing carries state in the workflow Context, which is the memory management the harness provides. This is a skeleton, your decompose, route, hybrid_search, rerank, and assess_sufficiency are where the real work lives, but the control flow is the thing to internalize.

8. Reranking Candidate Chunks With Jev

Retrieval casts a wide net on purpose: hybrid_search pulls 20 candidates so you do not miss the right one. But you cannot stuff 20 chunks into the answer prompt, that is slow, expensive, and dilutes the signal. You need to reorder them by true relevance and keep the best handful. That is reranking, and it is one of the single highest-leverage quality improvements in any RAG system.

A rerank asks a focused question about every candidate: given this query, how relevant is this specific chunk, as a score? This is exactly the shape of a decision, not a generation, which is why a System 1 model like Jev fits so well here. Jev takes unstructured state in and returns a typed, calibrated probability out, no text generated, which makes it fast and cheap enough to score many candidates per query. Scoring 20 chunks with a frontier chat model would be slow and costly; scoring them with a decision model is near-instant and near-free on the output side, and the calibration means a 0.9 relevance genuinely tends to be more relevant than a 0.6, so you can threshold on it.

def rerank(chunks, query, keep=8):
    # Jev-style decision model: score each chunk's relevance to the query.
    # Returns a calibrated probability, not text, so it is fast and cheap.
    scored = []
    for c in chunks:
        relevance = jev_score(            # typed probabilistic decision
            state=f"QUERY: {query}\nCHUNK: {c['text']}",
            question="Is this chunk relevant and sufficient to help answer the query?",
        )                                  # -> e.g. 0.87
        scored.append((relevance, c))
    scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True)
    return [c for score, c in scored if score > 0.5][:keep]

The pattern to carry away: use the big generative model to write the answer, and a fast calibrated decision model to make the many small relevance judgments along the way. That division of labor, generator for prose, decision model for decisions, is exactly the two-speed system design the whole field is moving toward, and reranking is its most natural home in RAG.

where

1. Models, Agents, and Harnesses, Quickly
Three words get used loosely, so pin them down before anything else, because agentic RAG is built out of all three.
A
model
is the raw reasoning: you give it text, it gives you text. An
agent
is a model placed in a loop where it can take actions (call a retriever, call a tool), see the results, and decide what to do next. A
harness
is everything around that loop that makes it work in production: the tools it is allowed to use, how its context and memory are managed, its permissions, and the rules that make it stop. In agentic RAG, retrieval is one of the tools in the harness, and the agent is the thing deciding when and how to use it. Keep this layering in mind; every later section slots into one of these three.
2. Traditional RAG: The Foundation You Still Need
Do not skip the classic pipeline, because agentic RAG is built on top of it, not instead of it. Traditional RAG is a fixed, linear sequence: embed the query, search a vector store for similar chunks, stuff the top matches into the prompt, and generate an answer.
This is one retrieval, one generation, no decisions. Its strengths are real: it is simple, fast, cheap, predictable, and easy to debug, and for a well-scoped corpus answering direct questions it is often all you need. Its limits are equally real. It always retrieves exactly once, so a question needing two facts from two places is already beyond it. It cannot decide that the retrieved chunks are irrelevant and try again. It cannot choose between data sources. And it has no notion of “that was not enough.” Every limitation agentic RAG removes is a limitation of this fixed shape, so understanding the shape is the foundation.
3. Chunking Strategies and Vector Search
Retrieval quality is set before the agent ever runs, by how you split your documents and how you search them. Get this layer wrong and no amount of agentic cleverness recovers it.
Chunking
is splitting documents into pieces small enough to retrieve precisely but large enough to carry meaning. The naive approach, fixed-size chunks, is easy and often cuts a sentence or an idea in half. Better approaches split on structure (headings, paragraphs) and meaning, and add a little overlap between chunks so an idea sitting on a boundary is not lost. The right chunk size is a genuine tradeoff: small chunks are precise but fragmentary, large chunks carry context but dilute relevance and cost more tokens.
Vector search
is how retrieval finds the right chunks. Each chunk is turned into an embedding (a vector that captures its meaning), the query is embedded the same way, and the store returns the chunks whose vectors are nearest. The crucial 2026 refinement, which carries straight into the agentic version, is that pure vector similarity is no longer the best you can do. Hybrid retrieval, combining semantic vector search with keyword search, plus a reranking step over the candidates, beats vector-only on almost every real workload. Hold that reranking thought; Jev enters there in section 8.
4. The ReAct Pattern and Reflection
Here is the engine of agentic behavior, and it is simpler than it sounds. ReAct stands for Reason, Act, Observe, a loop the agent runs until it is done.
Each turn, the agent
reasons
about what it knows and what it still needs,
acts
by calling a tool (in RAG, usually a retriever), and
observes
the result. Then it decides: is this enough to answer, or do I loop again? That loop is the entire difference between a search box and a researcher. The search box runs the pipeline once; the ReAct agent keeps pulling the thread until the question is actually answered.
Reflection
is the safety valve on top. When the agent notices it is stuck, repeating itself, or getting irrelevant results, a reflection step asks it to step back and critique its own approach before trying again, rather than grinding the same failing action. Reason-Act-Observe gives the agent forward motion; reflection keeps that motion from becoming an infinite loop of the same mistake. Both are cheap to add and transform reliability.
5. Traditional RAG vs Agentic RAG
Now put the two side by side, because choosing between them is the most consequential decision in the whole design.
Traditional RAG is a straight line: one retrieval, one answer. Agentic RAG is a loop with judgment inside it: the agent decides whether to retrieve, what to retrieve, from which source, and whether what came back is sufficient, looping until it is. The agentic version handles questions that need multiple facts, comparisons across sources, lookups that depend on earlier lookups, and cases where the first retrieval misses. The cost is real and worth stating plainly: agentic RAG is slower, more expensive (every loop is more model calls and more tokens, which compounds exactly as the context tax predicts), and harder to debug. The engineering judgment is knowing which questions actually need the loop, and section 10 is about exactly that.
6. Query Decomposition, Routing, and Multi-Hop Retrieval
Three specific agentic capabilities do most of the heavy lifting, and they are worth naming precisely because they are where agentic RAG earns its cost
Query decomposition
breaks a complex question into simpler sub-questions the system can answer separately, then combines them. “What is the best time to visit Japan and what should I pack” is really two questions, and splitting them retrieves far better than treating the mix as one search.
Routing
sends each question to the right source. Weather goes to a weather index, visa rules to the policy documents, hotel availability to a bookings database. A traditional pipeline has one source and no choice; the agent picks the right tool for each part.
Multi-hop retrieval
chains lookups where each answer feeds the next. “What are the must-see events in the capital of the country hosting the next World Cup” cannot be answered in one search, you first retrieve the host country, then its capital, then events there. Each hop depends on the previous one, which is impossible for single-shot RAG and natural for a ReAct loop. These three are the capabilities that justify going agentic.
7. A Travel Assistant, Step by Step, in LlamaIndex
Make it concrete with a travel assistant, the kind of query that genuinely needs the agentic loop: “I have four days in Japan in April, plan it around the cherry blossoms, I am vegetarian, and keep it under a budget.” That is decomposition, routing, and multi-hop all at once. from llama_index.core.workflow import (
    Workflow, step, Context, StartEvent, StopEvent, Event
)

class SubQuestions(Event):
    questions: list[str]

class Retrieved(Event):
    chunks: list[dict]      # each: {text, source, score}

class Reflected(Event):
    sufficient: bool
    missing: list[str]

class AgenticRAG(Workflow):
    @step
    async def plan(self, ctx: Context, ev: StartEvent) -> SubQuestions:
        await ctx.store.set("query", ev.query)
        await ctx.store.set("seen_ids", set())          # for duplicate prevention
        subs = await decompose(ev.query)                # LLM: split into parts
        return SubQuestions(questions=subs)

    @step
    async def retrieve(self, ctx: Context, ev: SubQuestions) -> Retrieved:
        seen = await ctx.store.get("seen_ids")
        chunks = []
        for q in ev.questions:
            source = route(q)                           # pick the right index
            hits = hybrid_search(source, q, k=20)       # semantic + keyword
            for h in hits:
                if h["id"] not in seen:                 # skip duplicates
                    seen.add(h["id"])
                    chunks.append(h)
        await ctx.store.set("seen_ids", seen)
        return Retrieved(chunks=chunks)

    @step
    async def reflect(self, ctx: Context, ev: Retrieved) -> Reflected | StopEvent:
        hops = await ctx.store.get("hops", default=0)
        reranked = rerank(ev.chunks)[:8]                # Jev reranking, section 8
        await ctx.store.set("context", reranked)
        judgment = await assess_sufficiency(            # reflection step
            await ctx.store.get("query"), reranked)
        # stopping conditions: answered, or out of hops
        if judgment.sufficient or hops >= 3:
            answer = await synthesize_and_verify(
                await ctx.store.get("query"), reranked)
            return StopEvent(result=answer)
        await ctx.store.set("hops", hops + 1)
        return Reflected(sufficient=False, missing=judgment.missing)

    @step
    async def replan(self, ctx: Context, ev: Reflected) -> SubQuestions:
        return SubQuestions(questions=ev.missing)       # multi-hop: chase the gaps
Read the steps top to bottom and the whole agentic pattern is visible: plan decomposes, retrieve routes and dedupes, reflect reranks and judges sufficiency, and either stops or loops back through replan to chase what is missing.

check is the stopping condition that keeps it finite;
seen_ids
is duplicate prevention; and the whole thing carries state in the workflow
Context
, which is the memory management the harness provides. This is a skeleton, your
decompose

route

hybrid_search

rerank

assess_sufficiency
are where the real work lives, but the control flow is the thing to internalize.
8. Reranking Candidate Chunks With Jev
Retrieval casts a wide net on purpose:
hybrid_search

You need to reorder them by true relevance and keep the best handful. That is reranking, and it is one of the single highest-leverage quality improvements in any RAG system.
A rerank asks a focused question about every candidate: given this query, how relevant is this specific chunk, as a score? This is exactly the shape of a decision, not a generation, which is why a System 1 model like
Jev
fits so well here. Jev takes unstructured state in and returns a typed, calibrated probability out, no text generated, which makes it fast and cheap enough to score many candidates per query. Scoring 20 chunks with a frontier chat model would be slow and costly; scoring them with a decision model is near-instant and near-free on the output side, and the calibration means a 0.9 relevance genuinely tends to be more relevant than a 0.6, so you can threshold on it.
def rerank(chunks, query, keep=8):
    # Jev-style decision model: score each chunk's relevance to the query.
    # Returns a calibrated probability, not text, so it is fast and cheap.
    scored = []
    for c in chunks:
        relevance = jev_score(            # typed probabilistic decision
            state=f"QUERY: {query}\nCHUNK: {c['text']}",
            question="Is this chunk relevant and sufficient to help answer the query?",
        )                                  # -> e.g. 0.87
        scored.append((relevance, c))
    scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True)
    return [c for score, c in scored if score > 0.5][:keep]

write the answer
, and a fast calibrated decision model to
make the many small relevance judgments
along the way. That division of labor, generator for prose, decision model for decisions, is exactly the two-speed system design the whole field is moving toward, and reranking is its most natural home in RAG.

This framework comes from a talk Daisy Hollman, an engineer on the Claude Code team at Anthropic, gave in the Build with AI Builder series. It is aimed at people already deep in agentic coding, and increasingly agentic knowledge work, who want to push past minutes of autonomy into hours and days. The core reframe is worth stating plainly, because it changes how you debug everything: an agent can run unattended for exactly as long as something other than you can say “wrong, try again” or “here is your next thing.” That something is a verification loop, and this post is how to build one that holds.

The only thing that does not scale as you try to get more done is your attention, so the way to do more is to run many agents at once, which means each one has to do productive work on its own between the few times you check on it. She runs up to dozens of sessions at a time; even without unlimited tokens, scaling to twenty concurrent sessions is very reasonable, and that only works if each session can run for hours without you. Verification loops are what make that possible.
