1. What an Agent Actually Is, and Why Loops Matter

Start with a definition, because the word gets thrown around undefined. The cleanest one: an agent is a model reacting to the output of its own tool calls. In 2022 and 2023 we had chatbots, your turn, the model’s turn, repeat. Then we realized the model could emit structured text (JSON, XML), we could act on it, and feed the result back as if it were another turn. Chain enough of those together, the model doing something, seeing the result, doing the next thing based on it, and at some point you call it an agent. There is no magic number of tool calls; “agentic” just means the model is reacting to what its actions produced.

The higher-order version is the one that matters for autonomy: the model runs many tool calls, then reaches the end of a workflow and needs some higher-level way to check its work and act on that check. In traditional software that check is CI, tests, or a benchmark. As agents move to higher-level and less code-adjacent tasks, that checkpoint gets fuzzier, but it never goes away. The goal of the whole design is simple to state: the inner loop (work, check, fix) should run many times, and the outer loop (the one that involves you) should run as few times as possible.

2. The Core Reframe: Fix the Loop, Not the Prompt

Here is the single most important instinct to retrain. When the agent reaches the review stage and something is wrong, your reflex should not be “let me prompt it again and restart.” It should be “how do I fix the loop so I never land here again, and the agent does not make this mistake again.”

The reason this matters is about where your leverage actually is. You have no control over the model’s weights or its raw intelligence. You can pick the best model available, but you cannot make the model itself smarter. What you can control is the process the model uses to produce output. “Don’t make this mistake again” is the only lever you have for scaling up the quality of agentic work. And this is not new: it is exactly how senior engineers made junior engineers better, and principal engineers made senior engineers better. We are applying a very old management practice to agents. The difference is that everyone is doing it now, without years of experience to lean on.

3. The Three Parts of Every Verification Loop

The framework breaks a loop into three components, and keeping them separate gives you something specific to examine when things go wrong.

The objective is what you actually want, the end state. It can be understated, underspecified, or, on the other side, too prescriptive: describing how to do it instead of what you want. Aim the objective at the what, and let the model choose the how.

The metric tells the model when its work is correct. In software that is usually unit tests, integration tests, or CI, but it can be any way to measure the quality of what was produced, including a document in knowledge work. If the work meets the metric, you are done and control returns to you.

The optimizer (Daisy frames it in mathematical terms as the gradient) is the direction the model should change the work to improve on the metric. This is the piece that turns a failed check into a better next attempt. And here is the subtle, critical point: the optimizer must stay in contact with the objective, not just the metric. If you steer only by the proxy metric, you overfit to it, which is exactly how you get a model that “fixes” a test by special-casing the test input in the code. The optimizer has to drive the implementation toward the real goal, not toward the measurement.

4. Why This Works: Verifier-Generator Asymmetry

Why should asking the model to try again produce something better than the first attempt? One rigorous reason is a formal result in computer science: verifier-generator asymmetry. Assuming P does not equal NP (set the technicalities aside), you can show that a great many problems are easier to verify than to solve.

Generalize that intuition from clean CS problems to coding, or even to knowledge work like writing a legal brief, and you can see, at least hand-wavily, why a model at a given level of intelligence might be better at checking correctness than at arriving at it. That gap is the whole engine of a verification loop: repeatedly checking correctness improves the part that keeps trying to reach correctness. It works with humans too; it just stands out far more at the scale of autonomy people are now pushing agents toward.

5. The Reinforcement Learning Parallel

The shape of this problem is not a coincidence; it is the same shape models are trained on. In reinforcement learning, the model gets a task and an environment, generates hundreds of attempts (really whole context windows of solving the problem, which all differ because the model samples probabilistically from its token distribution), and a grader scores each attempt. That grader can be another model, or something mechanical like a test result or benchmark. Then the weights are nudged to make the good attempts more likely and the bad ones less likely.

That should look exactly like a verification loop, because it is the same shape. The difference at inference time, when you are the one building the loop, is that you cannot change the weights. You have to change behavior with instructions: a skill file, a prompt, or honestly just a markdown file where you tell the model to write down its learnings and read them at the start of every task. Daisy is deliberately not prescriptive about the mechanism; skills are only slightly more structured than that markdown file. What matters is that this step leans heavily on the model’s own judgment about what it did wrong and what it could write down to avoid that failure next time, compactly, without filling the whole context window. That introspection is genuinely hard, and she notes models are only recently getting consistently good at it (she calls out Fable 5.1 as a notable jump), while smaller models still struggle. Getting good at building these loops now, as models improve, puts you far ahead when models that can do this reliably become common.

6. Verification Loops vs Hill-Climbing Loops

You will hear two terms, verification loops and hill-climbing loops. The assertion here is that for coarse or abstract tasks they are the same thing, with the same three parts; what differs is where the difficulty concentrates.

A verification loop is the familiar software shape: keep working until the tests pass, a clean yes-or-no. But many real tasks do not decompose into that. “Make the button purple” has a simple verification loop. “Make my website prettier” is a hill climb: the metric is not binary, you keep improving until it stops getting better or clears some quality bar. As Claude put it in Daisy’s own retelling, most real tasks are hill climbs wearing a checkbox. There is rarely one single thing that makes a senior-engineer-level task “done,” whereas a junior task is easy to hand off with “just make these tests pass.” The most efficient developers are moving toward treating their agent loops like senior or even principal engineers: pushing tasks to higher levels of abstraction, being very clear about the parts they care about, and letting the model handle everything else. Finding that threshold and going right up to it is where a lot of the productivity comes from.

7. Getting the Objective Right

Now each part in turn. For the objective, the question is how well you describe the end state and the things that actually matter about it. The most common mistake is wasting effort describing how to get there, when the model knows how, and often knows a better way than you do.

Planning is interesting here because it has shifted roles. A year ago it was popular because models would get halfway through and realize their approach did not work, so laying out the “how” up front gave better results. Now that models are more robust, planning is useful for a different reason: cleaning up an inexact objective. You often do not realize which parts you actually care about until you have a conversation, and planning surfaces that. So use planning to clarify the objective, but avoid using it to script the method.

This is also why the /goal command (in Claude Code, and in some other harnesses) became popular: it builds the whole loop out of just an objective. You write the end state; it creates a metric where a second model qualitatively introspects whether the goal is met; and the optimizer is the main model acting on that second model’s verdict. From writing only the objective, you get a verification loop. It is not the most robust loop and it will not handle the most abstract tasks, but it is surprisingly robust for many, and all you had to specify was the end state.

Your job is to be the clear-headed senior who decides what to build, understands each choice, and checks that the result actually does what you meant. This post is how to play that role well, so you end up with an app you can explain, not a black box you are afraid to touch.

https://maven.com/aishwarya-srinivasan/mastering-ai-agents

You can get an app on screen from one sentence now. The Shift: Your New Role in the AI-Assisted SDLC

The adjustment is learning how to give direction when you are no longer typing every line yourself. A coding agent can read your project, make changes, run tools, inspect the results, and try another approach. But it still needs a clear problem, and that is your job.

Think about briefing a colleague. If you say “build me a dashboard,” they have to make a lot of decisions on your behalf: who uses it, what information matters, what happens when there is no data. The same thing happens with an agent. You can delegate the implementation while staying involved in those decisions. That is the whole software development lifecycle (understand, design, implement, test, release, improve), and with an AI-assisted SDLC the agent helps throughout it: it can question your requirements, explain unfamiliar technology, implement a feature, and investigate a failure.

A Quick Tour of Codex: Projects, Plan Mode, Goals, Skills

Before building, get oriented in the surfaces you will use. Codex lives in the ChatGPT desktop app (download it from chatgpt.com, sign in, and select Codex from the ChatGPT dropdown).

Create a local project called Application Tracker and attach an empty folder, which is where the code will live. Inside it, start a new chat; later you might keep separate chats for planning, building a feature, and debugging, giving each the files and decisions it needs. These tools matter most.

  1. Plan mode (/plan) is where Codex investigates, asks questions, and helps you decide an approach before writing anything.

  2. Goal mode (/goal) gives it a persistent objective and a definition of “finished” that it works toward across turns, within its permissions, while you steer or pause.

  3. Skills are reusable instructions you can create (ask the skill creator to turn a checklist into one) and invoke again from the Skills sidebar.

And you can build from a sketch: draw a rough layout, attach the image, and describe what the buttons should do. Planning decides the work; a goal carries it through.

Check out my YouTube video on using Codex from scratch:

Define a Small, Useful First Version

Open a new chat in the project and turn on Plan mode. The discipline here is to describe behavior and set a clear boundary, so the agent is not guessing at scope.

Here is my actual first prompt:

“Help me plan a job application tracker for personal use. I want to add an application, update its status, and filter by status. Applications must still be there after I refresh the page. Start with a local development version using fictional data. Ask me about missing requirements before suggesting the implementation.”

Notice two things. I am describing behavior, not technology. And I am setting a boundary: a personal development version first, not accounts, resume analysis, email integrations, or auto-applying. Those come later. If Codex suggests extra features, push back:

“Which of these are necessary for the first version? What can we postpone without making the core workflow unusable?”

Then define a few things you can actually check. These are acceptance criteria, and they give both you and the agent a concrete way to decide whether the feature works:

Use the Agent as a Teacher Before Choosing the Stack

Now discuss technology, and here is the move most people miss: use the agent to teach you before you let it decide for you. Be honest about what you know. If you only know Java, say that. If you have never programmed, say that too. You do not need to pretend to understand a recommendation.

“I know Java, but I’m new to web development. Explain the parts this application needs. Compare two reasonable stacks. Tell me what each component does, what I would need to learn, and what we can avoid adding.”

Treat the answer as the start of a conversation, not a verdict. If it recommends a separate Python service, ask what that service would do. If an explanation is unfamiliar, anchor it: “Use our Save button as the example and explain one step at a time.”

For this example we can use Next.js with TypeScript and a Postgres database. The frontend is the form and list you touch in the browser; the backend receives requests, validates them, and talks to the database; Next.js builds both pieces in one project; TypeScript describes the kinds of values the code expects (a status should come from an agreed set); Node.js is the runtime that runs the server-side JavaScript, not another language; and Python is a language we could use but do not need here. That last decision matters: a stack should have a reason for every piece. When Codex recommends a package, interrogate it:

“What problem does this solve? Could we use something already in our stack? Check the current official documentation before recommending a version.”

And you can ask it to teach through comparison, which makes unfamiliar code much easier to approach: “Show me how this TypeScript function relates to something I would recognize in Java. Explain the differences that matter here.”

Choose a Database Based on the Work

Say Codex mentions Neon, Postgres, and BigQuery. Before choosing, understand what the names represent, because some of them are not even alternatives to each other. Postgres is a database system; Neon offers managed Postgres, so they are not competing options in the same sense. BigQuery is built for analytical workloads over large datasets. Our tracker mostly saves individual applications, retrieves them, and updates status, so I would choose Postgres, with Neon as a managed option.

Investigate the decision instead of accepting it:

“Compare managed Postgres on Neon with BigQuery for this application. Focus on frequent individual writes, setup effort, operating cost, and maintenance. Explain what future requirement would make us reconsider.”

A good answer ties the choice to your workload. Then settle the data before any code:

“What data do we need to store? Show me an example record before creating the database.”

For v1, a record needs a unique ID, company, role, status, and application date. And settle the small details that quietly change behavior: should the date store just the day, or the exact time? For this tracker, a calendar date is enough. You are already making software design decisions, even though you have not written the database code yourself.

Sketch the Interface and review the Architecture

Before building, draw three things: an Add Application button at the top, status filters underneath, and a list of applications. Paper and a photo is fine; the sketch can be rough. Then give Codex the behavior the drawing cannot show:

“Use this sketch as the layout reference. On mobile, show each application as a card. Keep the company and role easy to scan. Show a helpful empty state before any applications exist. Explain what happens while saving and if saving fails.”

That is what having an opinion about your interface means. You do not need to know the styling syntax to decide that an error should appear next to the field that caused it. Now ask for the architecture and read it as a journey:

“Based on our decisions, create an architecture diagram. Show the browser, server, and database. Trace what happens when I save an application. Label where validation happens and where credentials are stored.”

Every arrow should represent something you can explain. Ask Codex to walk through one real example including a failedsave, and confirm database credentials stay on the server. One subtlety worth internalizing: even if the browser checks for a blank company, the server must check it too, because someone can send a request without using your form, and TypeScript’s development checks do not validate incoming data by themselves. Ask the agent to show where those checks actually happen.

Build One Complete Slice

Now switch out of Plan mode and build the smallest complete journey: enter an application, save it, see it after refreshing. One slice end to end beats half of everything.

First, check the environment. The ChatGPT app gives you the agent; your application still needs its own tools (here, Node.js and the project’s packages):

“Inspect this project folder and check the tools needed for our agreed stack. Explain anything missing, using current official installation guidance. Keep project dependencies inside this project.”

If installation fails, give Codex the exact error and ask it to find the cause before trying another command. Next, create a separate development database through Neon, and handle the connection string carefully: it contains credentials, so enter it privately in your local environment configuration and keep it out of screenshots, chat messages, and source control. Have Codex create the project structure and the agreed table, review the changes, then save a Git checkpoint with secrets excluded. Git records versions of your source so you can inspect or undo changes; it does not back up your database. Then the first implementation milestone:

“Build the application form and list using our agreed architecture and Postgres table. Use fictional data. Validate company and role on the server. Show a saving state and a useful error if saving fails. Run the relevant checks and start the local preview. Leave filtering and status editing for the next milestone.”

Open the address Codex gives you (localhost means it is running on your own machine). Add a fictional application (Acme, Data Engineer, Applied), save it, refresh, and confirm the record is still there. Then try a blank company and confirm you get a useful validation message. If the record disappears after refresh, the screen may be updating while the save or load path still needs work, so ask Codex to trace that path before adding anything else. Once this works, you have a complete feature to build on.

Learn the Codebase as You Build

You now have code you did not write line by line, and you still need to navigate it. Use the agent to teach you the map, read-only.

“Read this codebase without changing it. What are the entry points for the home page and the save request? Explain how the application starts, and point me to the relevant files.”

I ask for entry points, plural, because a web app has different places where page rendering and server requests begin. Then build the map and ground it in reality:

“Explain the module structure. Which files handle the interface, input validation, database access, and tests? Give me a short map with file references.”

“Create an architecture diagram from the code as it exists now. Compare it with our planned architecture and flag any differences.”

That comparison matters: the planned diagram shows intention, the code-grounded one shows implementation. Then go deep on one path by following a single concrete input through it:

“Explain the function that saves an application. What does it receive? What does it return? What calls it? What happens if the database request fails?”

Trace company Acme, role Data Engineer, status Applied through that function, and make sure you can say in your own words: it receives the details, checks them, asks the database to save, and returns a saved record or an error. If the code behaves differently from the plan, have Codex explain the actual path rather than repeat the intention. These same prompts work when you inherit someone else’s codebase; you do not have to read every file in order.

title: Tokenomics: The Economics of Tokens, and How to Stop Your AI Bill From Exploding
author: Aishwarya Srinivasan
content_html:
Most teams understand their cloud bill and have no idea how their AI bill is shaped. Then an agent ships, the context grows every turn, reasoning tokens pile up invisibly, and the invoice is five times the estimate. Tokenomics is the discipline of understanding and controlling what you pay per token, and it is the difference between an AI feature with healthy margins and one that quietly loses money on every call. Here is the whole model, with the math and the code.

AI models charge you by the word-piece, called a token, both for what you send in and what they send back. Two things surprise people.

  1. First, the reply is usually several times more expensive per word than the question, so a chatty model costs more than a terse one even when it “knows” the same thing.

  2. Second, in a back-and-forth or an agent, the model has no memory between calls, so your program re-sends the entire conversation every single turn. That means the tenth message pays for the first nine again. Tokenomics is just learning where the money actually goes so you can stop paying for things you do not need.

Everyone building on LLMs eventually gets the same unpleasant surprise. The prototype cost a few cents. The production feature, at real volume with real conversation lengths, costs orders of magnitude more, and nobody can quite explain where it went. The reason is almost always that the team reasoned about cost the way they reason about a normal API, a flat price per call, when LLM cost is a function of token volume that grows in ways that are easy to miss.

If you want to upskill yourself in building Agentic Ai Systems - do checkout our TGA All Access Pass:

https://maven.com/aishwarya-srinivasan/mastering-ai-agents

This post is the mental model and the math for token economics. Not a price list, prices change weekly and vary by provider, so I will use clearly-labeled illustrative numbers and teach the structure that stays true. By the end you will understand exactly what drives your bill, why agents are the dangerous case, and the concrete levers that cut cost without cutting quality, with a cost calculator you can run.

Index

  1. First Principles: Why You Pay Per Token

  2. The Input-Output Asymmetry

  3. The Context Tax: Why Conversations and Agents Explode

  4. The Hidden Line Items: Reasoning Tokens and System Prompts

  5. Prompt Caching: The Biggest Lever Most Teams Ignore

  6. The Cost Formula, and a Worked Example

  7. Build It: A Token Cost Calculator

  8. The Optimization Playbook, in Priority Order

  9. Unit Economics: Does Your AI Feature Actually Make Money?

  10. Linkstash

First Principles: Why You Pay Per Token

A token is the unit a model reads and writes in, roughly a word-piece. “cat” is one token; “tokenomics” might be three. The reason you are billed per token rather than per call is that tokens are the direct driver of the model’s actual cost: compute scales with how many tokens the model has to process and produce.

The single most important habit in tokenomics is to stop thinking in “requests” and start thinking in “tokens in, tokens out.” A request is not a unit of cost. A request is a container for a variable, often large, and often growing, number of tokens. Two calls to the same model can differ in cost by 1000x depending on how many tokens each one moves. Once you internalize that your bill is tokens x price, summed over input and output, everything else follows.

The Input-Output Asymmetry

Here is the first thing that trips people up: input and output tokens are not priced the same. Output tokens typically cost several times more than input tokens, often in the range of three to five times, because generating is more expensive than reading.

The practical consequences are large and often counterintuitive. A model that “thinks out loud” at length, or pads answers with preamble and restatement, is burning your most expensive tokens. Asking for a concise answer, or constraining the output format tightly, is not just nicer to read; it directly cuts the pricier half of your bill. This is also why decision models and structured outputs are so economically appealing: when the output is a single label or a small typed object instead of a paragraph, you are spending almost nothing on the expensive side. The lesson: you have the most leverage over the output, so control it deliberately.

We hosted Haritha Thilakarathne from NVIDIA for a guest lecture on “Tokenomics”. Watch the session recording:

https://thegenacademy.com/lesson/ai-tokenomics-explained

The Context Tax: Why Conversations and Agents Explode

This is the mechanism that causes the surprise bills, and it is the single most important idea in the whole post. Models are stateless. They remember nothing between calls. So to continue a conversation, your code must re-send the entire history every single turn.

Read that carefully, because it is where agents get dangerous. In a ten-turn conversation, you do not pay for ten short messages. You pay for turn one ten times, turn two nine times, and so on, because each turn re-sends all prior turns as input. The total input tokens over a session grow roughly with the square of its length. An agent that runs twenty tool-calling steps, each re-sending the full and growing transcript plus tool outputs, can spend more on re-reading its own history than on any actual work. This is why a chatbot demo is cheap and a long-running agent is not: the context tax compounds. title: The Open-Source Multiverse
author: Aishwarya Srinivasan
content_html:
A frontier lab ships a new kind of model on a Monday. By the following week there is an open-weights version you can run on a MacBook, with the benchmark reproduced and the weights on Hugging Face under Apache-2.0. This is not a fluke. It is becoming the default metabolism of the field, and it quietly rewrites what is defensible in software. Here is what is really happening, and what it does not mean.

When a company builds something clever with AI, the clever part is usually the idea, not a secret only they can keep.

Once they describe what they built and how well it scores on a test, other people can rebuild something that behaves almost the same, often cheaply and in the open, for anyone to download.

It is a bit like a chef publishing not the exact recipe but a photo of the dish and its calorie count: skilled cooks can reverse-engineer a version that tastes nearly identical within days. That is now happening to AI products constantly. The result is a growing “multiverse” of free, open copies shadowing every paid launch, and it changes what a company can actually keep for itself.

In September 2026, TypeSafe AI shipped Jev, a new kind of model that outputs typed, calibrated probabilities instead of text, a “System One” decision model. It was a genuinely novel idea.

Within days, an open-weights reimplementation called Lev appeared: a 4-billion-parameter model built on an open base, trained on a single H100, running on a laptop, with the weights and the evaluation harness released under Apache-2.0. Not a leak. A clean-room reconstruction of the behavior, built in the open, in about a week.

Lev is not an isolated event. It rhymes with a pattern now repeating across the whole field: open reimplementations shadowing closed launches so fast that the two almost share a release date. People are gesturing at this with a cluster of names, Lev as open Jev, OpenMuse, OpenDot, and more arriving monthly. The individual projects matter less than the dynamic they reveal, which is the real subject of this post: we have entered an open-source multiverse, where for nearly any capability a lab demonstrates, an open version materializes almost immediately. That has deep consequences for what software is, what stays defensible, and the limits of the seductive phrase “you can reverse-engineer anything.”

Before we get into the code, one invitation: We are hosting /build-with-AI, a free online Global AI Builder summit, Which has over 10,000 people registered for the sessions. Join us at builders.gen-labs.ai. If you want to build production-grade agents with me and a lineup of people who ship this for a living, come build with us. This post is a taste of what that looks like.

Index

  1. The Anchor Case: How Lev Cloned Jev in a Week

  2. The Reproduction Template, Step by Step

  3. Why This Got So Fast, So Suddenly

  4. The Multiverse: OpenMuse, OpenDot, and the Pattern

  5. What “Reverse-Engineer Anything” Actually Means, and Does Not

  6. What Is Still Defensible When Capability Is Not

  7. The Future of Software This Implies

  8. The Honest Risks and Open Questions

  9. Linkstash

The Anchor Case: How Lev Cloned Jev in a Week

Start with the concrete, well-documented example, because it shows the whole mechanism in miniature. Jev, from TypeSafe AI, is a closed, proprietary decision model. Lev, released by Interfaze (a YC company), is its open-weights counterpart, and the details are the interesting part.

Lev is roughly 4 billion parameters: an open Qwen3.5-4B base plus a LoRA adapter, and per its own repository it was trained on a single H100 and runs comfortably on a MacBook or a small GPU. Its defining trick is the same one that makes Jev fast, described in Lev’s own terms as a “label-token readout”: the model “does not generate its answer by appending tokens; it reads the probability from the logit of a label token it already knows.” You hand it a decision state and a typed question (yes/no, choice, score), and it returns a single calibrated probability, say 0.83 for an escalation, where calibrated means that number should track real frequency: about 83 of 100 similar cases would be “yes.”

On S1Bench, the evaluation board for this class of model, Lev reportedly hits about 71.9% on the public subsets, topping the 4B-and-smaller class and landing slightly below Jev while being faster. It ships the weights, the LoRA adapter, and the measurement harness, with one honest caveat its authors flag: some training datasets may carry non-commercial licenses.

There are already multiple community forks under the “lev” name, and a separate “openjev” built on a different open base (DiffusionGemma). One closed idea, a constellation of open reconstructions, within days.

The Reproduction Template, Step by Step

What makes Lev worth studying is that it is a repeatable recipe, not a one-off. The same four moves reconstruct a surprising range of closed capabilities.

The crucial realization is that the hard, expensive part was having the idea and proving it works. Once a lab publishes that a new behavior is possible and shows a benchmark that captures it, they have handed the open community the two scarcest ingredients: the target and the proof it is reachable. From there, open base models are abundant and excellent, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (a LoRA adapter) is cheap enough to run on one GPU, and matching a benchmark is a concrete, gradient-friendly objective. The reconstruction does not need the original weights or data. It needs the concept and a yardstick, both of which a launch announcement typically gives away for free.

This is why “trained on one H100” is the most important phrase in the Lev writeup. The reproduction barrier did not just lower. For a whole class of capabilities, it fell to something a single motivated engineer can clear in a weekend.

https://maven.com/aishwarya-srinivasan/mastering-ai-agents

Why This Got So Fast, So Suddenly

Open reimplementations are not new. What is new is the speed, closing from months to days. Several forces compounded at once.

Each of these alone would help. Together they are a phase change. Open base models are now close enough to the frontier that you start most of the way there. LoRA-style fine-tuning turns “retrain a model” into “train a small adapter on one GPU in hours.”

A public benchmark converts a fuzzy capability into a precise, optimizable target. The launch blog that announces the closed product hands over the one genuinely scarce input, the knowledge that this specific thing is possible and roughly how. And AI coding assistants mean a single person now ships what used to take a team. Put them together and the time from “closed launch” to “open clone you can run locally” collapses toward zero.

The Multiverse: OpenMuse, OpenDot, and the Pattern

Lev is the cleanest example, but it is one star in a constellation, and the constellation is the point. Across categories, closed launches are now routinely shadowed by open projects, often several at once sharing a name.

A fair caution on naming: “OpenMuse” and “OpenDot” are each used by more than one unrelated project, so treat them as labels for a pattern rather than single canonical tools. Broadly, OpenMuse-style efforts are open takes on agentic personal assistants that can operate your computer, and OpenDot or OpenDots-style efforts are open alternatives to closed agent-automation products, including one notable design built around fully reversible, snapshotted agent actions. The specifics vary and some are early. What they share with Lev is the move: see a closed capability, rebuild it in the open, release it for anyone to run and fork.

The mental model to carry away is not “these three tools.” It is that every closed launch now casts an open shadow, often within the same news cycle, and the shadow is forkable, inspectable, and free. That is the multiverse: not one open alternative per product, but a growing, branching set of them.

What “Reverse-Engineer Anything” Actually Means

Here is where honesty matters most, because the slogan oversells and undersells at the same time. Be precise about what this dynamic can and cannot reproduce.

content_html:
OpenAI just put its weight behind a new category: models built to make one bounded decision inside your code, not to chat. The concept is important and the direction is real. The catch is that the Decisions API is a limited preview with no published spec, so most of what you can build today uses tools that already exist. This post explains the idea honestly and gives you runnable code for the pattern, not a fabricated API.

In simple English, first. Normally you ask an AI a question and it writes you a paragraph, and your program has to read that paragraph and try to pull an answer out of it. A “decision model” flips that. You hand it the situation and a short list of allowed answers, and it just points at one of them, fast, with a number for how sure it is. It is the difference between asking a colleague to “write me a report on whether this email is spam” and simply asking them to press one of two buttons: spam, or not spam. Same intelligence, far less fuss, and your code gets a clean answer it can act on.

At DevDay 2026, OpenAI announced the Decisions API, its entry into a category that TypeSafe AI’s Jev opened earlier in the year: models that exist to make a single, bounded decision inside software rather than to produce open-ended text.

OpenAI’s framing, from Sam Altman, is simple: “it works by giving our Luna model a predefined set of options to choose from.” The underlying model is GPT-6 Luna, OpenAI’s cheap, fast model, pointed at a narrow job.

This is a genuinely useful idea, and it is worth understanding precisely. It is also, right now, more announcement than product: as of this writing OpenAI has published no endpoint, no schema, no SDK method, no pricing, and no confidence-field documentation. The honest consequence is that nobody can show you a real Decisions API request body yet, and anyone who does is making it up. So this post does two things. It explains the concept and why it matters, accurately. And it gives you real, runnable code to build the same behavior today with APIs that actually exist, so “build your first examples” means something you can run tonight.

1. The Core Idea: Bound the Answer Space Before Inference

Here is the one sentence that captures why decision models are architecturally interesting, and it is worth reading slowly: a decisions endpoint bounds the answer space before inference, whereas structured outputs constrain the format of generated text after the fact.

A normal LLM call generates a stream of text and you hope it lands on something you can parse. Even with structured outputs, the model is still generating a sequence and being shaped to fit a format. A decision model starts from the other end: the set of valid answers is fixed before the model runs, so the model’s entire job is to pick one. That reframing is what unlocks the speed (there is far less to generate), the reliability (the answer is always one of your options), and the clean fit into code (you get a value, not prose to parse).

The mental model OpenAI and TypeSafe both push is the “smart if-statement”: a place in your program where hand-written rules are too brittle to capture the real distinction, so you drop in a fast, bounded, model-made decision instead.

2. Decision Models vs Structured Outputs, the Distinction That Matters

If you already use OpenAI’s structured outputs, you might ask what is new here. The difference is subtle and real, so let us make it exact.

Structured outputs are the right tool when you need the model to produce something with shape: extract five fields, fill a form, return a nested object. Decision models are the right tool when you need the model to choose one thing from a known set, over and over, fast and cheap. One generates a constrained artifact; the other selects from an enumerated space. In practice the line blurs, and the example code below shows that you can get most of the decision-model behavior today by using structured outputs with a tightly bounded schema. The Decisions API’s bet is that making “choose from this set” a first-class operation, rather than a special case of generation, is worth a dedicated endpoint.

3. The Four-Step Design OpenAI Describes

OpenAI frames the right way to use decision models as a four-step loop, and it is good discipline regardless of which tool you use.

Two of these steps are where teams go wrong, so they are worth stressing. Step two, define a bounded question, means the question has to be specific enough that two reasonable people would agree on the correct answer. “Is this good?” is not a decision; “Does this reply resolve the customer’s stated issue, yes or no?” is. Step four, enforce in code, means you treat the model’s decision as evidence feeding your own policy layer, not as an authority that acts on its own. The model says “route to billing, 0.91”; your code decides what to do with that, including when to ask a human. That separation is what keeps a probabilistic decider safe inside a real system.

4. What Is and Is Not Known About the Decisions API

Being precise here matters, because the gap between the announcement and the product is wide, and a lot of writing about it quietly fills that gap with invention.


What is confirmed: the Decisions API is a limited-preview endpoint backed by GPT-6 Luna, it accepts text or images, and OpenAI’s DevDay slide claims roughly 150 milliseconds per call against about 1.6 seconds for a standard Luna call, which they frame as a 10x speedup against their own cheapest model. Their product lead described it as “less than a few hundreds of milliseconds end to end.”

What is not published, as of early October 2026: the endpoint path, the authentication, any SDK method, the request or response schema, whether it returns option probabilities or just a pick, context limits, and decision-specific pricing. The underlying Luna model is priced around $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, but whether decisions are billed the same way is undisclosed. The practical takeaway is blunt: you cannot build against the Decisions API yet, and any code sample claiming to show its request body is fabricated. That is exactly why the build section below uses APIs that are actually documented.

5. How It Compares to Jev

OpenAI is not first here. TypeSafe AI’s Jev defined the “System One model” category earlier in 2026, and the contrast is instructive because the two took different routes to the same idea.

Jev is a ground-up model that architecturally cannot produce free text; it only returns typed, calibrated decisions, it is generally available with real SDKs and published schemas, and it prices output tokens at zero. The Decisions API is a frontier LLM (Luna) constrained to a bounded answer space; the underlying model can still generate text, it is in limited preview with nothing published, and it arrives with OpenAI’s distribution and ecosystem behind it.

The honest summary: Jev is the more radical and more finished version of the idea, and the Decisions API is the more cautious version from the vendor with the most reach. The category is now real enough that the biggest lab in the space validated it, which is the most important signal of all. To learn more about Jev, check out my blog:

Build Example 1: A Decision Model Today, With Structured Outputs

You do not have to wait for the Decisions API to build decision-model behavior. You can do it right now with OpenAI’s documented structured outputs by bounding the answer space with an enum. This is real, runnable code.

from openai import OpenAI
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Literal

client = OpenAI()

# Step 2 from the four-step design: define the bounded question
# as a schema whose answer space is a fixed set of options.
class RoutingDecision(BaseModel):
    category: Literal["billing", "technical", "account", "spam"]

def decide_route(ticket_text: str) -> str:
    # Step 1: capture state. Step 3: select from the answer space.
    completion = client.chat.completions.parse(
        model="gpt-6-luna",            # a cheap, fast model is the right fit
        messages=[
            {"role": "system",
             "content": "Classify the support ticket into exactly one category."},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        response_format=RoutingDecision,
    )
    return completion.choices[0].message.parsed.category

# Step 4: enforce in code. The decision is an input to your policy.
route = decide_route("I was charged twice for my subscription this month.")
print(route)   # -> "billing"

The Literal type is doing the real work: it tells the model the answer must be exactly one of four strings, so you can never get back a malformed or out-of-set value. That is the decision-model guarantee, available today. The whole function is a “smart if-statement”: where a pile of brittle keyword rules used to route tickets, one bounded model call does it.

title: Jev and the Idea of “System One Models,” Explained
author: Aishwarya Srinivasan
content_html:
Almost every model you use was built to talk to a human. Jev, from TypeSafe AI, is built to be called by code. It takes unstructured state in and returns typed, calibrated, probabilistic decisions out, with type errors ruled out by construction rather than by prompting. The idea is sharp and worth understanding, and the numbers deserve a careful read. Here is both.

There is a quiet mismatch at the center of how most people use LLMs in production. The models were trained and shaped for conversation, fluent, flexible, open-ended text for a human to read. But a huge share of real deployments are not conversations at all.

They are a program calling a model to make one small decision inside a workflow: classify this ticket, route this request, score this output, extract these fields, decide this branch.

We take a system optimized for open-ended dialogue and bolt it into a control-flow slot, then spend enormous effort forcing it to return clean JSON and not make things up.

Jev, the first release from TypeSafe AI (founded by Diogo Almeida, previously on ChatGPT research at OpenAI), is a bet that this slot deserves its own kind of model. TypeSafe calls it a “System One Model,” and the framing is the interesting part: a model built for automation inside software rather than for interaction with people. This post explains what that means, how the architecture is said to work, what the claims actually are, and, because the numbers are extraordinary, how much weight to put on them.

Before we get into the code, one invitation: I am hosting /build-with-AI, a free online Global AI Builder summit, at builders.gen-labs.ai. If you want to build production-grade agents with me and a lineup of people who ship this for a living, come build with us. This post is a taste of what that looks like.

  2. Why “System One”: The Kahneman Framing

  3. Typed Probabilistic Decisions, Concretely

  4. The Architecture: Parallel Sampling and RLCD

  5. The “No Hallucination” Claim, Read Carefully

  6. Calibration: The Underrated Part

  7. The Performance Claims, and How to Weigh Them

  8. What You Would Actually Build With It

PS: I have recorded a detailed video on Jev on my YouTube as well, so if you would like to take a look at it, you can find it here

1. The Core Idea: A Frontier-Intelligence Function Call

The single sentence to anchor on is TypeSafe’s own framing of what Jev is:

“Think of Jev as a frontier-intelligence function call: unstructured state in, typed probabilistic decisions out.”

Sit with that, because it inverts the usual mental model. A chat LLM is a thing you talk to. Jev is a thing your code calls, like any other function, except the function body is frontier-grade intelligence.

Everything distinctive about Jev follows from taking that function-call metaphor completely seriously. A function has a typed signature, so the output is a type-safe structured value, not free text. A function should be fast and cheap to call, so the design optimizes hard for latency and price. And because the decision is probabilistic, the function returns not just an answer but a calibrated confidence on that answer. It is less “a smaller chatbot” and more “a new primitive for putting intelligence inside a program.”

2. Why “System One”: The Kahneman Framing

The name is a deliberate borrow from Daniel Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow. System 1 is fast, automatic, intuitive thinking; System 2 is slow, effortful, deliberate reasoning.

The industry has spent the last two years pouring effort into System 2: reasoning models that think longer, deliberate over chains of thought, and trade seconds or minutes of latency for harder problem-solving. TypeSafe’s argument is that a large class of production decisions do not need System 2 at all. They need a fast, reliable, well-calibrated judgment, made hundreds of times per second, cheaply, inside a loop. That is a System 1 job, and a model purpose-built for it looks nothing like a reasoning model. The positioning is a genuine fork in the road: not “a better general model,” but “a different model for a different half of the brain of your software.”

We’ll cover GenAI foundations, RAG, agentic design patterns, fine-tuning, evaluations, and AI safety, with a project every week across two tracks: low-code/no-code for non-developers and code-heavy for developers. 3. Typed Probabilistic Decisions, Concretely

The phrase “type-safe structured values” is the technical heart, so make it concrete. Instead of prompting a chat model and hoping it returns parseable JSON, with Jev you define the possible outputs and their structure in advance, and the model returns a value that conforms to that structure by construction, each field annotated with a probability.

The examples TypeSafe shows make the range clear: a decision workflow that outputs probabilities across multiple fields at once, selecting the best Wikipedia link out of a large set of choices (they cite up to 255 options), and evaluating a game state to produce probabilistic branching decisions. The unifying idea is that the shape of the answer is fixed before the model runs, and the model’s job is to fill that shape with calibrated probabilities rather than to compose prose. For a developer, this is the difference between “parse and pray” and “call a typed function.”

4. The Architecture: Parallel Sampling and RLCD

TypeSafe attributes Jev’s behavior to three architectural choices. The blog is upfront that the deep algorithmic details are deferred to future writeups, so treat this as the shape of the approach rather than a full spec.

  • A structured-output-first architecture. Rather than a general text model with structured output grafted on, the model is built around producing typed values.

  • A parallel sampler. This is the most consequential departure. A standard LLM generates output one token at a time, sequentially, each token conditioned on the last, which is why long outputs are slow. TypeSafe says Jev “generates all outputs in a single query” in parallel. If the answer is a fixed-shape structured value rather than an open-ended string, you do not need autoregressive left-to-right generation, and dropping it is where much of the claimed speed comes from.

  • RLCD: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions. Where RLHF optimizes for human preference and RLVR optimizes for verifiable correctness, TypeSafe describes RLCD as optimizing specifically for “answers with epistemically honest probabilities on System One tasks.” In other words, the training objective is not just “be right” but “know how right you are,” which is what makes the confidence numbers meaningful rather than decorative. The specifics of the algorithm are not published yet, which is worth noting.

5. The “No Hallucination” Claim, Read Carefully

This is the claim that will get the most attention, and it needs the most careful reading, because TypeSafe is actually fairly honest about its nature if you read closely.

The precise claim is “0% type errors,” and TypeSafe is candid that this number is guaranteed by construction, not measured empirically. Their own words: schema matching is guaranteed, so they “can confidently add 0% into the plots,” and they note it is “not empirical.” That distinction matters enormously, so let us be exact about what it does and does not mean.

What it does mean: if you define an output as a boolean or a choice among a fixed set, you will always get back a valid boolean or a valid member of that set. Everyone is talking about AI, ChatGPT, and agents, and almost no one explains how any of it actually works in plain English. If you have ever felt overwhelmed by the jargon, this is your complete crash course. No prerequisites, no hand-waving. By the end you will understand the landscape and know your first concrete step.

There is a growing AI literacy gap, and it is not your fault. The field buries newcomers under acronyms, LLM, RAG, fine-tuning, agents, tokens, and assumes you already know the difference between the AI in a spam filter and the AI in ChatGPT. Those are genuinely different things, and nobody tells you that.

So let us close the gap from the ground up. This post does four things.

  1. It walks through the evolution of computers in four stages: rule-based systems, machine learning, deep learning, and finally the generative AI we use today.

  2. It demystifies the terminology so the words stop being intimidating.

  3. It is honest about what GenAI can do and what it cannot do safely, hallucinations, privacy, and bias.

  4. It gives you a prescriptive path to get started, sorted into three tracks, plus a beginner exercise you can try in five minutes.

Think of this as the one-stop starting point I wish existed when everyone around me started saying “GenAI.”

If you prefer a video way to learn things, you can also check out my YouTube video on “Gen AI Explained.”

You could also do both, the way I would recommend is going through the blog once (skim it), then watching the video, and then coming back to the blog for more nuanced takes

The Four Stages of AI, at a Glance

The single most clarifying idea for a newcomer is that “AI” is not one thing. It is the result of decades of evolution in how ywe make computers behave intelligently, and it arrived in four stages, each solving what the previous one could not.

The through-line is who writes the logic and what the system produces.

A human writes explicit rules, then machines learn to predict from examples, then they learn to recognize deeply complex patterns in images and speech, and finally they learn to create brand-new content. Each stage did not erase the last, all four are in use today, but each unlocked something new. Understanding what separates them is the foundation for everything else.

Before we get into the code, one invitation: I am hosting /build-with-AI, a free online Global AI Builder summit, at builders.gen-labs.ai. If you want to build production-grade agents with me and a lineup of people who ship this for a living, come build with us. This post is a taste of what that looks like.

Stage 1: Rule-Based Systems

The oldest approach, and still everywhere. A human sits down and writes explicit instructions: if this happens, do that. The intelligence lives entirely in rules a person wrote by hand.

A classic spam filter that blocks any email containing certain banned words is rule-based. So is a tax-calculation program, a thermostat, and most of the business software running the world. The strengths are real: it is predictable, fully transparent (you can read exactly why it did what it did), and it needs no data to build, just a human who knows the rules.

The limitation is where it fails in messy, real-life scenarios: it can only handle situations someone anticipated and wrote a rule for. The moment reality produces a case the rules did not cover, the system has no idea what to do. And for a problem like “is this photo a cat,” the number of rules you would need is effectively infinite, nobody can write down every rule that separates a cat from a dog in pixels. That wall is exactly what the next stage was invented to climb.

Mastering Agentic AI Certification
I’m hosting a 6-week Mastering Agentic AI Certification with my co-founder, Arvind Narayan, designed for both technical and non-technical professionals who want to build deep, practical expertise in AI systems. We’ll cover GenAI foundations, RAG, agentic design patterns, fine-tuning, evaluations, and AI safety, with a project every week across two tracks: low-code/no-code for non-developers and code-heavy for developers. No prerequisites are required, and over 35% of our current cohort comes from non-coding backgrounds.

Enroll here: https://maven.com/aishwarya-srinivasan/mastering-ai-agents?promoCode=SAVE20

Stage 2: Machine Learning

Instead of a human writing the rules, you show the machine many examples and let it learn the patterns itself, then use them to make predictions. This is the key shift: the logic is discovered from data, not handwritten.

Show a model thousands of photos labeled “cat” or “dog,” and it learns the patterns that separate them. Then it can classify a photo it has never seen. This is the AI behind product recommendations, fraud detection, credit scoring, and the demand forecasting that runs supply chains. It is enormously powerful and still the right tool for a huge share of real problems.

What defines this stage: it learns from examples to predict or classify. It outputs a label (”spam” or “not spam”), a number (”this house is worth 340,000”), or a probability. What it does not yet do well is handle the really complex, high-dimensional patterns in raw images, audio, and language. That is the leap of the next stage.

Stage 3: Deep Learning

Deep learning is machine learning powered by neural networks with many layers, and it is what let computers finally recognize genuinely complex patterns: the objects in an image, the words in speech, the structure of language. It is the stage that made modern AI possible.

The idea that makes deep learning special is that the network learns in layers, building understanding from the ground up. Early layers pick out simple features (edges, sounds), and later layers combine them into complex ones (faces, words, meaning), all learned automatically from data rather than specified by a human. This is the technology behind photo tagging, voice assistants understanding your speech, and language translation.

Deep learning matters here for one reason: it is the direct ancestor of generative AI. The same layered-neural-network approach that learned to recognize complex patterns turned out, at enormous scale, to be able to generate them. Stage four is stage three, scaled up and pointed at creation.

Stage 4: Generative AI

Generative AI learns patterns from truly enormous amounts of data, so deeply that it can generate new content: text, images, audio, video, code. This is the era of ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, image generators, and the tools everyone is suddenly talking about.

The defining difference is in the name: it generates. Where earlier stages recognize or classify (this photo is a cat), generative AI produces something new that did not exist before, a poem, an image, a working function, an answer phrased just for you. It learns from vast, mostly unlabeled data (much of the public internet), and you interact with it in plain language: you prompt it, and it responds.

That combination, learning from enormous data and generating new content on demand from an ordinary-language request, is what makes this stage feel like magic and what makes it genuinely new. It is not smarter than earlier approaches at everything; for many narrow prediction tasks, a small traditional model is still cheaper and better. What GenAI unlocked is the ability to create and to be directed in plain human language. That is the whole revolution in one sentence.

title: How to Do Agentic Data Analysis in 2026
author: Aishwarya Srinivasan
content_html:
Agents can now retrieve a dataset, clean it, run exploratory analysis, train a baseline, and write the report, with no human touching the procedural steps. So the question everyone is asking is fair: is the data scientist obsolete? The short answer is no, but the job has changed shape, and the reason why is the most important thing in this post.

Something genuinely shifted at the intersection of AI and data science, and it changed how the work gets done. The systems deployed today do not just generate an answer and stop. They plan, they execute multi-step tasks, they call tools, they evaluate their own outputs, and they loop back when results fall short. An agent can now retrieve a dataset, scrub it, run exploratory analysis, train a baseline model, evaluate results, and produce a structured report, all without a human intervening during the procedural steps.

That capability naturally provokes the anxious question in the title. If the machine can do the whole pipeline, is the data scientist finished? I want to answer that honestly, because both the doom take and the dismissive take are wrong. The procedural work of data science is genuinely being automated.

But the judgment work, the part that was always the actual science, is becoming more important, not less. This post is two things at once: a prescriptive guide to doing agentic data analysis well, and a clear-eyed answer to whether the profession survives it. The two turn out to be the same story.

Index

  1. What Agentic Data Analysis Actually Is

  2. The New Workflow: You Orchestrate, Agents Execute

  3. A Prescriptive Pipeline You Can Actually Run

  4. The Hard Truth: Agents Make Bad Analytical Decisions

  5. The Garden of Forking Paths, and Why Judgment Cannot Be Prompted Away

  6. So Is Traditional Data Science Dead? The Honest Answer

  7. The Skills That Now Matter Most

  8. Changing the Educational Landscape

  9. A Prescriptive Checklist for Trustworthy Agentic Analysis

  10. Linkstash

1. What Agentic Data Analysis Actually Is

Start with the distinction between the old AI tools and the new ones, because it is the whole ballgame. A standard LLM is a very smart but passive reference book: you ask, it answers, it stops. An agent is a proactive junior colleague: you give it an objective, and it goes off to pursue it, taking multiple steps, using tools, and reporting back.

In a data context, an agent is not just generating code snippets. You can hand it an objective like “improve the accuracy of the customer cancellation model,” and it will test different algorithms, engineer new features, validate the results, and come back with findings. It monitors, investigates causes, and delivers insights, where traditional BI tools and copilots wait for you to ask the right question. That autonomy over the procedural steps is what “agentic” means here, and it is real. The wins are documented: teams report dramatically faster pipeline development, audit processes cut from days to an hour, and analysts freed from data wrangling to do actual analysis.

2. The New Workflow: You Orchestrate, Agents Execute

The shape of a 2026 data science project is not “human does the work” and it is not “agent does the work.” It is a division of labor, and knowing which parts belong to whom is the core skill.

The human owns the ends: framing the real business question at the start, and judging the results at the end. The agents own the middle: the procedural execution, often as a small team of specialized agents (a data-cleaning agent, an EDA agent, a modeling agent) coordinated by an orchestrator, working in parallel and logging their progress. Crucially, note where the human gates sit. Validation can be automated; promotion is not. Drift can trigger a retraining proposal automatically, but a human approves or rejects it. The loop keeps running, but the consequential decisions stay with a person. That is not a temporary limitation. As we will see, it is the point.

AI with Aish is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

3. A Pipeline You Can Actually Run

Here is how to actually stand up agentic analysis, in the order I would build it. This is the prescriptive core.

Three of those steps are the ones people skip and regret.

  1. Frame the question yourself: An agent handed a vague goal optimizes for a plausible-looking answer, not the right one, so the precision of your objective and success metric bounds the quality of everything downstream.

  2. Give it a frozen environment: reproducibility is not optional in analysis, and running the agent in a pinned, containerized environment is what lets you trust that a result can be regenerated.

  3. Force it to red-team its own conclusion: this single step, making the agent argue against its own finding before it surfaces it, is the difference between an analysis you can trust and one that just sounds confident.

Everything else, the cleaning, the exploratory analysis, the modeling, the agent genuinely can do well and fast. Your leverage is concentrated at the framing, the constraints, and the review.

4. The Hard Truth: Agents Make Bad Analytical Decisions

Now the part the vendor demos skip, and the part that answers the title question. AI coding agents write flawless code and make unreliable analytical decisions. Those are two completely different skills, and conflating them is the central mistake of the moment.

A documented 2026 finding makes this vivid: given identical datasets, autonomous agents produced wildly divergent conclusions across runs, with different runs frequently reversing whether a hypothesis was even supported. In direct testing, a vanilla coding agent confidently recommended a wrong budget reallocation. A framework built to enforce analytical rigor, exploring many modeling approaches instead of one, correctly returned “no valid model found” on a case where the naive agent had happily produced an answer.

Sit with that. The failure mode is not that the agent writes buggy code. The code runs perfectly. The failure is that the agent makes a judgment call, one of the hundreds of small analytical choices every real analysis requires, and makes it badly, then presents the result with total confidence. Plausible and correct are different things, and an agent optimized to produce plausible output will cheerfully hand you the wrong answer with a clean chart attached.

5. The Garden of Forking Paths, and Why Judgment Cannot Be Prompted Away

The reason for that failure has a name, and understanding it is what separates people who use these tools well from people who get burned by them.

Every analytical workflow is a series of judgment calls: how to treat outliers, which features to include, which model family to try, how to handle missing values, where to set a threshold. This is the “garden of forking paths.” A vanilla agent walks one path through that garden and delivers the answer at the end of it, with no indication that a different set of equally defensible choices would have led somewhere else, possibly to the opposite conclusion.

This is why the problem cannot be solved with a better prompt. The issue is not that the agent misunderstood you. It is that the space of defensible analytical choices is large, the choices interact, and picking well among them requires domain knowledge, statistical judgment, and epistemic humility, exactly the things that are hard to specify and easy for a confident model to fake. The fix is structural, not verbal: force the agent to explore multiple paths, measure the sensitivity of the conclusion to the choices, and red-team its own finding before surfacing it. Judgment has to be built into the system, because it cannot be prompted into the model.

6. Changing the Educational Landscape

If the job is being rewritten toward judgment, orchestration, and validation, then the way we teach data science comes under pressure too, and this is where the conversation gets genuinely contested. The tempting conclusion is that curricula should pivot hard toward high-level orchestration and away from the mechanical fundamentals that agents now handle. But that conclusion is exactly where a careful educator would slow you down.

I put this question to Tanvir Ahmed Shaikh, Director of AI Systems and Adjunct Professor at Carnegie Mellon University | CMU, who spends his time bridging industry and academia and training the next generation of AI leaders. I want to answer that honestly, because both the doom take and the dismissive take are wrong. The procedural work of data science is genuinely being automated.
But the
judgment

procedural

The shape of a 2026 data science project is not “human does the work” and it is not “agent does the work.” It is a division of labor, and knowing which parts belong to whom is the core skill.

title: 4 Months Left in 2026: Here Is Your 100-Day Plan for AI Upskilling
author: Aishwarya Srinivasan
content_html:
No theory dumps. No 40-course reading lists you will never finish. This is a sequenced, build-first plan with a concrete deliverable every two weeks. Follow it in order, ship the artifacts, and by December you will have a portfolio that proves you can do AI engineering, not just talk about it.

There are about 100 working days left in 2026. That is enough time to genuinely change your trajectory as an AI engineer, but only if you stop consuming and start building. The single biggest mistake I see in AI upskilling is treating it like a subject to study rather than a craft to practice. You do not become an AI engineer by watching a course. You become one by shipping systems that work, breaking them, and fixing them.

Before we get into the code, one invitation: I am hosting /build-with-AI, a free online Global AI Builder summit, at builders.gen-labs.ai. If you want to build production-grade agents with me and a lineup of people who ship this for a living, come build with us. This post is a taste of what that looks like.

So this plan is heavily prescriptive on purpose. Every phase has an exact focus, a set of concrete actions, and a shippable deliverable. If you only have an hour a day, this works. If you have more, it works faster. The rule is simple: you are not allowed to move to the next phase until you have shipped the current phase’s artifact. Consuming content without producing an artifact is how 100 days evaporate with nothing to show. Let us not do that.

  2. The Arc: Five Phases, Five Artifacts

1. How to Use This Plan (Read This First)

Four rules make this work. Break them and the plan degrades into another course you half-finished.

The most important rule is the second one. The artifact is the checkpoint, not the calendar. If it takes you 25 days to ship the phase-one app instead of 20, fine, you are still on track, because the deliverable is what matters. What is not fine is reaching day 20 having watched everything and built nothing. Consuming feels like progress and is not. Building is the only thing that compounds.

One more thing: work in public. Every artifact goes on GitHub with a real README. Every phase, write a short post about what you built and what broke. This is not vanity. The portfolio and the public track record are the outcome you are working toward. A hiring manager cannot see the courses you watched. They can see the systems you shipped.

2. The Arc: Five Phases, Five Artifacts

Here is the whole plan on one page. Five phases of 20 days, each producing one portfolio-worthy artifact, each building on the last.

The sequence is deliberate and non-negotiable. You cannot meaningfully build an agent (phase 3) before you understand retrieval and context (phase 2), and you cannot understand retrieval before you can make a basic LLM call reliably (phase 1). And you should not put anything into your portfolio as “production-grade” until phase 4 teaches you what that actually means. Do them in order. The compounding is the point.

3. Days 1 to 20: Foundations and Your First Real App

Focus: stop being a chatbot user and become someone who builds on the model programmatically. By day 20 you will have a deployed app that calls an LLM through code

.

  • Days 1 to 5, API fundamentals. Get an API key (Anthropic, OpenAI, or an open model via a gateway). Write a Python script that makes a call and prints the response. Then learn the primitives that actually matter: system prompts, messages, temperature, max tokens, streaming, and how token cost is calculated. Do not touch a framework yet. You must be able to make a raw API call and explain every parameter before you let a library hide it from you.

  • Days 6 to 10, prompting and structured output. Learn the real prompt-engineering toolkit: few-shot examples, chain-of-thought, clear role and task framing, and above all structured output, forcing the model to return valid JSON against a schema. This is the single most useful production skill in the phase, because real apps need parseable output, not prose. Practice until you can reliably get schema-valid JSON out of the model every time.

  • Days 11 to 15, build the app. Pick one narrow, real problem and build a small app around it. Not a demo, something you or a friend would use: a tool that summarizes and tags your saved articles, a script that turns meeting notes into action items, a resume-tailoring tool. Keep the scope tiny and the utility real.

  • Days 16 to 20, deploy and document. Put it somewhere it runs without your laptop open (a serverless function, Streamlit, a small server). Write a README that explains what it does, how it works, and what you learned. Commit it to GitHub.

Phase 1 artifact: a deployed LLM-powered app with a real README. You now build on models instead of just chatting with them.

Enroll here: https://maven.com/aishwarya-srinivasan/ai-for-forward-deployed-engineers?promoCode=30OFF

4. Days 21 to 40: Retrieval and Context Engineering

Focus: ground a model in data it was never trained on. By day 40 you will have a working RAG system that answers questions over your own documents with citations.

Days 21 to 25, the retrieval primitives. Learn embeddings, similarity search, and chunking, what they are and why they matter. Understand the pipeline: documents get chunked, chunks get embedded, a query gets embedded, and you retrieve the closest chunks. Build a tiny version by hand before reaching for a vector database, so you understand what the library does.

Days 26 to 30, build basic RAG. Assemble a working retrieval-augmented generation system over a document set you care about: your notes, a set of PDFs, a codebase. Question in, retrieved chunks plus answer out. It will be mediocre at first. That is expected and instructive.

Days 31 to 35, upgrade retrieval quality. This is where you learn what separates toy RAG from real RAG. Add hybrid retrieval (semantic plus keyword search) and a reranker to reorder candidates by true relevance. Measure the difference on a handful of test questions. Pure vector search is no longer state of the art, and feeling that improvement yourself is the lesson.

Days 36 to 40, citations and ship. Make the system cite its sources, every answer points back to the chunk it came from, and add a verification pass that flags unsupported claims. Deploy it, write it up, commit it.

Phase 2 artifact: a RAG system with hybrid retrieval, reranking, and inline citations. You can now ground models in private data, the core skill behind most real AI products.
